The Compendium of the Essence of Yoga
I bow to Gaṇeśāna, the destroyer of obstacles to the recitation of the Praṇava;
I worship him who is gracious, the bestower of desired objects, and the cutter of worldly existence.

I bow to the Guru, the illustrious Dakṣiṇāmūrti, whose lotus-face possesses the immeasurable luster of ten million moons, who is ever-mindful of the moon, and who is skilled in bestowing the nectar of Rājayoga.
Śrī Śaṅkara, Parāśakti, Gaṇeśa, Ṣaṇmukha,
Hari, Brahmā, Nandikeśa, Dattātreya, and Patañjali.

I worship the multitude of the lords of new yogis, Vyāsa, and the son of Vyāsa; I salute the mother of Brahmā and Viṣṇu— the queen swan sporting in the forest of the foundational lotus, the streak of lightning residing in the great inner sky, the lightning of bliss, and the consort of the enemy of Ananga (Śiva).
She who is easily reached by the flame issuing from the lotus-mouth of the *mūlādhāra*, embraced by that [flame],
possessing the luster of a thousand times ten million rising suns, resembling a fine thread, transcending the mind (*unmanī*),
and constantly intent on the desire for union with Sadāśiva, who has transcended all principles (*tattva*).
I meditate upon Śrī Kuṇḍalī, who generates splendor by means of the principles (tattvas).
Whose lotus-feet are the swans that have cast off sleep,
whose divine limbs are adorned with jewels of excellent complexion,
whose eyes are the sun, wind, and moon, and who is the sole seed of all—
I worship my mother, whose form is sprinkled with supreme nectar.
Her auspicious limbs resemble a mass of vermilion; she is eager for dalliance upon the left lap of Śiva,
her gentle smile cherished by him alone.
I worship Gaurī for the sake of crossing over worldly existence.
It is the supreme lotus of all yogas beginning with the eight limbs, belonging to the illustrious Kuṇḍalinī;
it is that which possesses the characteristic of the path capable of bursting open the door-panels of the Brahma-gate;
and it is the very nature of the Self, the abode of Sadāśiva who transcends all principles (tattvas).
I shall reveal all of that which was previously described in the yogas.
Having thoroughly examined all the treatises on yoga, I shall here set forth the essence of yoga in summary, out of a desire to favor those who practice it.
This scripture is proclaimed for those who follow the path taught by the guru, who adhere to the teachings of the Yoga-shastra, and who are endowed with detachment and virtuous conduct.
As it has been said in the Yogaśāṅkara:
"Having made firm the sword of knowledge and the shield consisting of dispassion...
In a rare battle for yoga, the hero shines forth at the pinnacle.
In the Gītā:
"By practice and by dispassion, O son of Kuntī, it is grasped.
Through yoga alone, embodied beings are liberated from the bondage of worldly existence.
Otherwise, there is no liberation for them even in hundreds of millions of births.
Thus it is stated in the Yogaśāṅkara:
"There is no liberation without yoga; that liberation which is shown by yoga, one who is joined with yoga knows, and is thus liberated from the ocean of existence."
The very cessation of the mind is designated as yoga;
by the power of the practice of yoga alone, the Supreme Self is revealed.
As it is said in the Śvetāśvatara Upaniṣad: "The mind should be restrained within the heart until it has reached its dissolution;
this is both knowledge and meditation, while all other things are merely the expansion of books."
And Patañjali [states]: "Yoga is the cessation of the fluctuations of the mind.
The internal organ is the intellect (*buddhi*) and the mind (*manas*); their fluctuation is what is called [the object of] yoga.
"My mind has gone elsewhere"—having said this, you ought to understand that which was spoken.
The activity of the mind is of two kinds, said to be either pure or impure;
the impure is the cause of birth, while the pure is the destroyer of birth.
As it is said in the Amṛtabindu Upaniṣad:
"The mind is indeed declared to be of two kinds: pure and impure.
The impure is characterized by desire and volition; the pure is devoid of desire."

"The mind alone is the cause of bondage and liberation for human beings; attached to sense objects it leads to bondage, while free from sense objects it attains liberation. Thus, through these two [means] alone, cessation occurs, just as darkness is dispelled by the sun and the moon.
Otherwise, the movement of the mind can never be restrained.
This was stated by Patañjali:
"The cessation of the fluctuations of the mind depends on both.
[As stated] in the Vyāsabhāṣya:
Its cessation is achieved through practice and dispassion.
The practice of yoga consists of cultivation and dispassion, along with effortless spontaneity;
through these two alone yoga is attained, and not through mantras and the like—of this there is no doubt.
Mantra, Haṭha, Layayoga, and Rāja—these are the fourfold types of Yoga.
Through understanding the meaning of these Yogas, one becomes liberated; not otherwise.
Withdrawal of the senses, meditation, breath control,
concentration, deliberation, and absorption— this is said to be the six-limbed yoga.
And this prima facie argument (pūrvapakṣa) first defines the eight ancillaries of yoga (yogāṅga), after which the nature of the mantras and other yogas is defined.
In the Sūtasaṃhitā—
Yama and niyama, as well as āsana,
O Brahmin, likewise prāṇāyāma, and furthermore pratyāhāra.
Retention (dhāraṇā), meditation (dhyāna), and concentration (samādhi) is the eighth, O Sage. Non-violence, truthfulness, non-stealing, celibacy, compassion, straightforwardness,
forbearance, fortitude, moderation in diet, and purity— these are the ten restraints (yamas).
O ascetic, apart from the manner prescribed in the Vedas,
there is neither injury nor non-injury by body, mind, or speech in any other way.
O Sage, the conviction that the self is omnipresent, indivisible, and incapable of being burned— that indeed is declared by those who know the Vedānta to be the supreme non-violence.
O best among the knowers of the Vedas, whatever is seen or heard by those with clear senses is the word of that very person; it shall be true, O Brahmin, and cannot be otherwise.
The conviction that "everything is the supreme Brahman and nothing else" is declared as the ultimate truth by those purified by the knowledge of Vedānta.
The wise know that non-stealing consists in the cessation of desire— even in one's mind— regarding the jewels, gold, or pearls belonging to another.
The avoidance of conventional usage regarding the existence of a self by means of its name—
this has been declared as non-stealing by the great-souled ones who know the Self.
The complete avoidance of women by means of body, mind, and speech—
except during the period following menstruation— is called celibacy (brahmacarya).
Chastity is likewise prescribed for those established in the stage of studentship (brahmacarya-āśrama), for ascetics (yatins), for lifelong celibates (naiṣṭhika),
and similarly for forest-dwellers (āraṇyavāsins).

Sexual union with one's own wife according to the prescribed rule during each fertile season is likewise declared to be the practice of celibacy (brahmacarya) for those dwelling in the householder stage of life.
Celibacy is proclaimed for the king, as well as for the householder; some learned men also desire it for Vaiśyas who follow their proper livelihood.
"Indeed, it has been proclaimed that for a Śūdra there is only the vow of service;
likewise, the highest form of *brahmacarya* consists in directing the movement of the mind toward the state of Brahman."
Regarding all beings as one’s own self through body, mind, and speech— this very compassion,
which is practiced with permission [by all], has been proclaimed by those who know the limbs of yoga;
it is to be maintained constantly toward friend, son, wife, enemy, and oneself.
O Sage, that which is uniform is called "straightness" by the wise;
yet she was tormented by enemies through her body, mind, and speech.
O bull among sages, that cessation of the agitation of the intellect is what constitutes forbearance (*kṣamā*).
For a sage, liberation from *saṃsāra* comes from the Veda alone, and not otherwise.
Thus, the accomplishment of consciousness is declared by the knowers of the Vedas to be fortitude—
that firm-mindedness which thinks, "I am the Self, and I am distinct from others."
This is declared by the sages who have mastered the Vedas and by the disputants to be the most excellent form of self-restraint;
however, for those who eat very little or have already finished their meal, this yoga is not possible in any way.
Therefore, food that is conducive to yoga is moderate eating. Viśveśvara says: Food that is wholesome, moderate in quantity, and that which does not cause indigestion—[this is moderation].
Therefore, one should avoid that food which causes the bodily elements (*dhātu*) to become disturbed.
In the *Yogasāramañjarī*:
"Through [unwholesome] diet, the yogi is cut off, just as the moon wanes during the dark fortnight."
Just as the moon waxes during the bright fortnight, so does his food intake increase.
In the Gītā:
"Yoga is not for him who eats too much, nor for him who does not eat at all. In the Sūta-saṃhitā:
O great sage, the external purification consisting of the removal of bodily impurities by means of earth and water is known as physical purity;
they know mental purity to be right reflection.
The wise desire purity that consists in the knowledge "I am pure";
a person who abandons the purity of knowledge delights instead in external [purity].
O observer of noble vows, like one who, being deluded, abandons gold and grasps at iron,
so it is with the yogi who has been purified by the water of knowledge and has accomplished his purpose.
"There is nothing that ought to be done in this world for one who knows reality; if there is something to be done, he does not truly know reality. Now, as for the rule—Yājñavalkya says:
Austerity, contentment, faith, charity, worship of the Lord,
listening to the established doctrines, modesty, intelligence, recitation of mantras, and vows.
These observances have been proclaimed by the high-souled masters of yoga;
I shall describe them to you in due order, so listen with faith.
That which consists of the emaciation of the body through the Kṛcchra, Cāndrāyaṇa, and other such methods prescribed in the Vedas is called *tapas* by the wise.
Whatever is obtained here by men spontaneously and constantly is sufficient;
the sages have declared that this is the characteristic of contentment.
Faith in dharma and adharma is called *āstikya*;
likewise, wealth and food acquired through righteous means [should be offered] with purity to a Vedic twice-born.
Whatever else is given away, that is declared by me to be *dāna*.
Whatever object is given to a Vedic Brahmin shines;
that which is given for the sake of a mere worldly favor would be like an oblation poured into ashes.
"Adoring Āditya, Ambikā, Viṣṇu, Gaṇanātha, and Maheśvara according to one's capacity and with devotion— that, O Lord, is true worship.
Thus it is said in the Sūtasaṃhitā.
A heart free from passion and the like, speech free from falsehood and other such faults,
and a body free from violence and the like— this is the worship of the Lord.
The wise should understand through the hearing of Vedānta that the inner self (pratyak) is truth, knowledge, infinite, supreme bliss, the highest, and eternal.
The wise have declared that listening to the Purāṇas is equivalent to listening to the established tenets (siddhānta),
provided that no action contrary to the Vedas or the Vedic path occurs therein.
The sense of shame that arises toward that [transgression] is proclaimed as *hrī*.
Furthermore, one should possess an intellect characterized by faith toward all Vedic matters;
even when instructed by a teacher, one should remain free from attachment to those worldly concerns.
The practice and recitation of mantras according to the very path declared in the Vedas is known as *japa*.
Likewise, whatever engagement there is with the *Kalpasūtras*, the Vedic scriptures, the Purāṇas, and the Itihāsas, that is called *japa* by me.
Those Smṛtis that are outside the Veda, and whatever false doctrines there may be—
all of them are declared to be fruitless and are known to be rooted in darkness (tamas).
In the Gītā:
"Better is one's own duty, though devoid of merit, than the duty of another well performed.
Death in one's own duty is better; the duty of another is fraught with fear. Thus it is said.
Therefore, one should always recite the *vedamanta* with all effort.
The syllable *ja* is the destruction of birth, and from the syllable *pa* comes the destruction of sin.
Because it destroys both birth and sin, it is called *japa* by the wise.
Recitation is said to be of three kinds: vocal, whispered, and mental;
the mental is declared to be performed with the mind, while the whispered is traditionally held to be performed with the tongue.
"Recitation aloud is vocal," says the best among those who know the Vedas;
"mental recitation is a thousandfold, while whispered recitation is said to be a hundredfold."
The vocal [recitation] is indeed one; it is declared that its characteristic is *japa*.
Viśvāmitra says:
"That which is with high, low, and circumflex tones, with distinct words and syllables..."
A Brahmin should utter the mantra; that is the vocal sacrifice of recitation (japa-yajña).
While reciting the prayer, one should repeat it with pure vowels, consonants, and words;
one should not shake the head or the neck, nor should one grind the teeth.
If heard in a low voice, it becomes Bhārgī; if not heard at all, it becomes fruitful.
One who constantly meditates upon the seer, the meter, the deity,
and the mantra while reciting the Bhārgī mantra, indeed obtains that very fruit.
"Having first been instructed by a gracious guru,
that which is performed with his permission for the sake of attaining dharma, artha, and kāma is called *vrata*.
Now, the sequence of postures (*āsana-krama*):
Now, for the benefit of practitioners, I shall indeed describe the sequence of postures (āsanas),
by the very practice of which stability becomes easily attained.
In the *Yogasāramañjarī*:
the Vīra, Kūrma, the very firm Svastika, Kukkuṭāsana, Mayūra, Vijaya, Padma, and likewise Vyāsāsana.

I shall now describe, according to the prescribed rule, the firm seat (dṛḍhāsana), the bull seat (vṛṣabhāsana), the seat of Garuḍa (gārūḍāsana), the elephant seat (gajāsanā), the perfected seat (siddhāsana), and the lion seat (siṃhāsana).
Having composed himself in a clean place, covered with a pleasant cloth,
he should properly place his right leg upon the left thigh.
Placing the neck, head, chest, and hands evenly one above the other,
and contracting the anus with one-pointed concentration— this is the supreme *vīrāsana*.
By means of this yoga of practice, one becomes established in yoga and attains perfection;
yet, for the sake of swift accomplishment, the mind must not be allowed to wander during the performance of the practice.
One should place his right shank upon his left thigh and the head [of the left foot] upon the [right] thigh;
this is to be known as the tortoise posture (kūrma-āsana), which brings all the senses under control.
Placing the right foot at the root of the left thigh,
one should arrange that foot upon the seat at the root of the right thigh to form a very firm posture.
Having extended both arms, it is called the Svastika posture;
O Goddess, it bestows all accomplishments and destroys all diseases.
Having placed the left ankle below and the right one above, and having pressed the anus with the feet,
one should cross the pair of knees.
Having placed [the fingers] at the bases of the fingers of the left hand according to the palm,
one should turn them over at the bases of the fingers of the right hand onto that same palm.
Pressing the two roots of the thighs, one should fix the eyes upon the tip of the nose;
this indeed is the cock posture (*kukkuṭāsana*), which is the cause of mental steadiness.
Having placed the pair of feet upon the two roots of the thighs...
Between those two, with the anus firm and the back raised, remaining motionless,
one should sit with the pair of palms joined together against each other.
Placing one thigh over the other, one should gaze at the nose;
this is indeed the Mayūra-āsana (Peacock Posture), which destroys all diseases.
One should position both arms like a pair of staffs.
One should place both palms on the ground in the shape of a hollowed cup;
with the body slightly bent, remaining motionless and with a steady mind.
Seated comfortably and with a concentrated mind, one should gaze at the beautiful feet;
this is the "Vyāsāsana," which immediately destroys disease and bestows the perfection of yoga.
Then, having placed the left foot upward upon the right thigh,
one should likewise place the right foot upon the left thigh; having positioned them thus,
one should leave the arms as they naturally rest upon the thighs.
One should place the back of the hand called "Dakṣa" within the interior of the left palm.
Having made the neck straight and the head erect, one should gaze at the tip of the nose;
neither closing nor opening the eyes, one should indeed contract the anus.
With body balanced and mind steady, one should practice this supreme lotus posture (padmāsana) for the sake of attaining all yogic success and for the destruction of worldly existence.
Having placed the right shank upon the left shank, with his senses subdued,
he should place the side of the ankle at the base of the right shank and abdomen.
From the *hastādi* posture up to the *mati* posture, one should perform them like the *padmāsana*;
for this is indeed the supreme *vijayāsana*, which grants all accomplishments.
Having carefully placed the pair of feet upon the thighs—
with the right foot on the left side and the left foot on the right side—
Having diligently rotated both hands behind the back,
one should firmly grasp both big toes with the two hands.
With the heart somewhat uplifted, one should gaze at the tip of the nose;
this is declared to be the firm posture (dṛḍhāsana), which instantly destroys disease.
O Maheśānī, having placed the right ankle upon the back of the left ankle, one should let both knees fall upon the ground.
Placing the elbows upon the thighs with the palms joined in the *añjali* gesture,
one should gaze at the tip of the nose while drawing the chin slightly toward the throat.
This indeed is the supreme Garuḍāsana, which bestows all accomplishments;
one should firmly press the earth with the anus and also clearly with both feet.
Placing both hands above the knees, one should remain with the body firm and steady;
this is the elephant posture (*gajāsana*), which brings about the destruction of all obstacles.
O Pārvatī, for the purpose of the root-seat (mūlapīṭha) joined with the thighs, one should embrace the shanks;
having placed the feet together at the back, the body becomes firm in the paryanka posture.
Pressing the anus with the heel, one should place the left [heel] over the private parts;
with the body balanced and having become steady, this is the supreme pure posture (śuddhāsana).
O Goddess, bestower of all accomplishments and destroyer of all diseases,
having caused him to fall, she closely embraced his pair of thighs with her two shanks.
Placing the two elbows like pillars, one should rest on one side;
this, O Goddess, is called by me the supreme Vṛṣabhāsana.
"This has been proclaimed by the Great-Souled Ones for the purpose of destroying all diseases. Thus it is said.
Now, the posture (āsana) determined by Ādinātha will be described;
one should practice that posture which bestows stability, health, and strength to the limbs and feet.
Having properly placed both soles of the feet between the knees and the thighs,
sitting with the body straight— this is described as the Svastika posture.
One should place the right ankle on the left side of the back, and likewise the left ankle on the right; this is the cow-faced (gomukha) posture, just as the face of a cow is turned.
Having pressed the anus with the two ankles in reverse order while remaining composed, this becomes the tortoise posture (kūrmāsana); such is the opinion of those who know the Vedas.
Having firmly established the lotus posture (padmāsana), one places the hands between the knees and the thighs.
Having placed it on the ground and established the kukkuṭāsana situated in the sky,
one should grasp the neck with both arms while remaining in the kukkuṭāsana posture.
This is the Uttānakūrmaka (the upturned tortoise posture), in which one lies supine like a tortoise;
having grasped the two big toes with the hands, [one extends them] as far as the ears.
The bow-drawing posture (dhanurākarṣaka) is described as follows:
having placed the right foot at the base of the left thigh and encircling both knees with the left arm, one stands;
this is the Parivartitā posture, which the Lord of Gomatsya taught. One should assume this seat.
The Matsyendra-pīṭha, expanded within the belly, is the weapon that shatters the circle of fierce diseases;
through practice, it bestows upon men the awakening of Kuṇḍalinī and their own pure essential nature.
Having extended the two legs on the ground like staffs and grasping the tips of both feet with the two arms,
with the forehead resting upon the knees— this they call *paścimatāṇa*.

If one practices the final breath-control (tāṇa) on the supreme seat of the west, causing the wind to flow through the western channel, the digestive fire within the belly shall blaze; men will experience leanness of the abdomen and freedom from disease.
Supporting the earth with both palms, with the sides of the navel resting upon the elbows,
rising from a high seat like a staff— this they call the Mayūra-pīṭha in the sky.
Lying upon the ground like a corpse on its back,
this corpse-posture removes the fatigue of all other postures and is the means for achieving mental rest.
O Pārvatī, they know this Siddhāsana to be the foremost among all postures; having bent the shanks and placed the feet joined together upon the seat of the thighs,
one should hold the body very firmly in the cross-legged posture (paryaṅka).
Pressing the anus with the heel, one should encircle the left side of the private parts.
O Goddess, having become steady with the body balanced, this supreme Siddhāsana bestows all accomplishments and destroys all diseases.
One should practice the perfected [path] within the eighty-four pīṭhas,
and likewise within the seventy-two thousand channels, such as the suṣumnā.
Meditating on the Self and restricting one's diet for as long as twelve years,
through constant practice of the Siddhāsana, one shall attain the perfection of Yoga.
When the Siddhāsana is attained, there is no need for many laborious postures;
for once the vital breath is held with vigilance in the Kevalakumbhaka, [all else follows].
And that Unmanī state arises spontaneously of its own accord, without effort;
likewise, when the Siddhāsana is always maintained even for a single moment,
the three knots are pierced spontaneously without effort.
There is no posture equal to *siddhāsana*, no breath-retention (*kumbhaka*) equal to solitary *japa*,
no mudrā equal to *khecarī*, and no dissolution (*laya*) equal to *nāda*.
Then one should place the two ankles upon the testicles;
the left ankle on the right side of the vagina and the right ankle on the left side.
Placing both hands upon the knees and extending the fingers,
with the mouth covered and the mind well-composed, one should gaze at the tip of the nose;
this is the Lion Posture (siṃhāsana), always honored by yogins.
One should place the ankles on either side of the scrotum;
then, having firmly bound the feet and sides with both hands, one remains motionless.
This Bhadrasana destroys all diseases;
indeed, the Siddha-yogins call this Gorakshasana.
The seat is said to be threefold:
dwelling in one place, the seat of kuśa grass and so forth, and the seat of the Siddhas and so forth.
One should dwell in one place for as long as the intended period;
beyond a distance of one *krośa*, one should not wander about—this is declared by the wise to be "immovable" (*acala*).
Having established a firm seat for oneself in a clean place—
neither too high nor too low, covered with cloth, a deerskin, and kusha grass.
Having made the mind one-pointed there, with the activities of the mind and senses restrained,
let him sit upon his seat and practice yoga for the purification of the self.
In the region of Badhipradeśa, within the expanse of the Marubhūmi desert, where the cry of "Sadāmaru" resounds,
in the land of Kīkaṭa— filled with anthills, teeming with many living beings, and abounding in Kirātas and petty kings.
In the *Yogasāramañjarī*:
[One should practice] on a riverbank or by the shore of the ocean, which is not crowded with gnats and mosquitoes and is frequented by wild beasts, but not in the vicinity of a pond.
"In a cremation ground, or at a sacred tree, but not in the presence of a great multitude;
in a region without a king, at a borderland, or in a place infested with anthills and the like. Thus it is said:
"In a pure, delightful, and guileless place, devoid of people..."
It should be cleaned, joined together, smooth, and free from depressions or elevations.
Regarding Haṭhayoga:
there, one should construct a beautiful monastery with a narrow entrance and free from cracks;
its enclosure wall should be well-built, pure, and provided with an external lattice.
It was strewn with fragrant flowers, adorned with canopies and awnings,
and filled with pillows, beds, seats, and other furnishings.
It is constantly perfumed with excellent incense and smeared with cow dung;
it is provided with sacrificial fuel, flowers, and leaves, and endowed with bulbs, roots, and fruits;
it is fully adorned with sacred ash, rudrākṣa beads, and water infused with kuśa grass.
"Filled with pure food and condiments, and containing all medicinal herbs. Thus [it is said].
In the *Haṭhayoga-śaiva*: "A cave with a small entrance, free from holes and pits, neither too high nor too low, nor too long..."
Properly smeared with thick cow-dung, stainless, and free from all defects;
beautiful on the outside with a pavilion, a platform, and a well, and surrounded by a wall—
this is declared to be the characteristic of a yogi’s monastery for those practicing haṭha for the sake of spiritual perfection.
Thus ends the first chapter, titled "The Determination of Restraints, Observances, Postures, and Places," in the *Yogasaṃgraha* composed by the venerable Dattātreya.
Having understood in detail the channels, their locations, their colors, and the functions of the vital breath (prāṇa), the lord of yogis should properly begin the purification of the channels.
In that regard, Śiva [says]: "Suṣumnā, Daśamadvārā, Harā, Dārā, Camadhyamā,
Nāgā, Candrā, Svargamukhī, Maśakā, and Madhyanāḍikā."
Pampālinī, Marākārī, Bālaśakti, Tapasvinī, Śaṅkhinī, Nalinī, Gaurī, Śikhinī, Vyāpinī, and Guhā.
The month-long fast, the triple city, the triple confluence, and the Mandākinī are the destroyers of all diseases.
That [goddess] is Kokilā, Abhrā, Japadā, Siddhā, and Vajrā; she is the tooth of the immortals, the void, and the boat.
Facing the formless, with its bulbous root directed toward the mouth, it is the fierce needle of withdrawal;
it is the Śaṅkhinī, the net of Śiva, the Jālandhra, and the celestial Gaṅgā flowing upwards.

In the upper west is Saritkārī, whose face is like a tawny ant; she is Ākulā, who praises the perfected sages. Thereafter follows the Maṇikula, the domain of Hari and Viriñci, which, despite its uneven joints, connects with the thread of the wind, possessing the splendor of the day.
She is the means for the liberation of the jewel of the Lord of Maru; she is the mistress here by mere union;
she is the lotus-like beloved of the gods; and she is also called the path of the lineage-jewel that unites the sky.
In the *Yogasāramañjarī* and the *Nāradīya*:
"At the door of Brahman, there are three knots: Vāmī, Kapālinī, and Trigandhi; all these together constitute the root-ornament (*mūlikamaṇḍanī*)."
Likewise, there are Mṛṇālatantra, Triliṅga, and Sarvarasa as well.
The Primordial Lord (Ādinātha). The channel situated in the center of the kanda is celebrated as Suṣumnā; around this wheel, channels extend from the feet to the head.
In the *Nārāyaṇa*:
"Constantly moving with its veins, resembling a sheath;
at its end is a subtle cavity, within which everything is established. Thus it is said.
She is called the Muktidevyāgama, the bestower of happiness and the sustainer of the universe;
she is self-established from the beginning, benevolent, pure, and stainless.
The channel situated in the middle of the back is always established at the crown of the head;
it is subtle, auspiciously Vaiṣṇavī, brilliant white, and known as Vijayā, the Manifested.
The tongue is the plowshare, the blue movement is the upward path, and she is exceedingly well-guarded.
Bhairava said:
She is known as Sudhā, she dwells in the center, she is Sarasvatī, the path of Brahman;
she is the abode of the three forms, the light of the world, and the source of all prosperity.
"She is accessible to yogis, bird-shaped, and has the form of the Mother Maṅgalā. Thus [says] Dattātreya:
"She is heaven, peace, and the transition (saṅkrānti); she is the cause and the sustainer of the universe."
She is the eternal abode of wisdom, the one to be attained, known by the name Kedārā.
"Kailāsa, Vaikuṇṭha, Kāla, Māsa, and Abda— these and many other names such as Viṣṇu are determined in the Yoga-śāstras. Thus [it is said] in the Śivayoga:
The speech of Brahmā and Indra is intoxicated by the passion of goodness (*sāttvika-mada*); the Vāṇī is as cool as a hundred thousand moons; the Candrā is like the Gaṅgā;
the Vāruṇī is like the Khadirā; and the Kalaṅkā is beautiful.
O best of Śivas, this very act of withdrawal shall be called by Your own name.
Piṅgalā is the lotus of the sun, Yamunā, fire, and day;
Iḍā is the left, the inhalation, and Piṅgalā is remembered as the right.
The Gaṅgā and the Yamunā, the moon and the sun, night and day,
as well as birth and death— these are declared to be the two fortnights.
Dharma and adharma are called the two dark and red [lines];
the white and black [lines] are known as the Varaṇā and Asi, the station of the two swans.
The station of Śiva-Śakti is situated on both sides of the Suṣumṇā.
The units of time—kalā, kāṣṭhā, and muhūrta—are the causes for those whose bodies are the universe;
they are manifest as the nature of the five elements and consist of the five Brahmans.
At the gateway of fragrance, in the practice of the arts, there are two flows caused by birth;
they are filled with excessive smoke and the letter *ya*, brought under control by the yogi, and eternal.
Joined with the mind, these two are the activators of the senses;
having the nature of *prāṇa* and *apāna*, they set in motion the activity of the world.
Consisting of two syllables, they are pure, yet they differentiate into various phonetic variations.
They are established in the five locations and consist of the three and five vital breaths.
For all living beings,
this vital breath (prāṇavāyu) is eternally the initiator of the body's duration, because it is the cause for determining time.
It exists in the form of breath within both the *iḍā* and the *piṅgalā*;
without these two, the living being does not remain—of this there is no doubt.
"The Suṣumnā is said to consist of the three fire-energies (kalās) at all times.
Humans do not know that the Suṣumnā is the vehicle therein;
by means of it, the gods and supreme yogis attain true knowledge. Thus [it is said].
In the *Praṇavacintāmaṇi*:
"The exhalation from the body extends twelve finger-breadths;
upon inhalation it reaches eight finger-breadths; in the middle [of the breath], it is lost at four finger-breadths."
In the *Śārīra*: "Three hundred and sixty breaths constitute one *nāḍikā*,
and five *nāḍikās* are proclaimed to be one zodiacal sign (*rāśi*)."
One knows the day by means of the twelve zodiac signs, beginning with Aries;
they are of the nature of mobile, fixed, and dual, and are joined with breath.
The four movable signs are situated on the left side; the fixed signs belong to the south; and both types of dual-natured signs are located in both places.
These are Aries, Cancer, Capricorn, and Libra.
These four signs are situated on the left side:
Scorpio, Taurus, Leo, and Aquarius; while [the remaining] are from the right side.
Virgo, Pisces, Sagittarius, and Gemini are situated on both sides;
they likewise determine the past, the present, and the future, as well as the auspicious and inauspicious results.
13) Within these zodiacal signs (*rāśi*), one should understand [the results] from the rising of the planets (*grahodaya*). In each individual sign here, there are five elements (*bhūta*).
Air, fire, earth, water, and space—
these five indeed constitute the airy and other channels for all the zodiacal signs.
The second channel is to be known [as the Āgneyī], the third is considered Pārthivā,
the fourth is to be known as Vāruṇī, and the fifth is remembered as Vyomākhyā.

The wind flows through the nose and the sides; it moves upward in the Vāyavya (north-western) portion and the remaining signs [of the zodiac]. It moves upward in the Āgneya (southeastern) portion, and in the Pārthiva (earthly) portion, it flows along the side of the pillar.
When the wind is below the nose, it occurs in the portion of Earth;
when the wind is in the middle of the nose, it clearly flows in the portion of Ether.
The preceptor (Jupiter) and the atom (Saturn) move in the northwest; Bhrigu (Venus) and Mars are in the southeast;
Mercury and Rahu are to be known as being on the earth; and the Moon and Saturn are in the water.
One should know that there is a conflict in the sky in all the zodiac signs;
and as previously stated, the benefics are always in the first [odd] houses, while the malefics are in the subsequent [even] ones.
Rāhu, Mars, the Sun, and Saturn—these are auspicious when situated to the south; Jupiter, Venus, Mercury, and the Moon—these gentle planets bring auspiciousness when situated to the left.
Malefics on the left bestow auspicious results, while these same benefics yield malefic fruits;
they grant auspiciousness during entry when on the left, but bring inauspiciousness during exit.

Thus, having always ascertained the auspicious and inauspicious results among the beings born under the zodiac signs according to the rising of the planets, the wise astrologer, when questioned, should then declare everything.
Wherever the wind is present, if one is questioned there, it is indeed auspicious;
if one is situated where the wind is absent, it would be in vain.
If one is in front and the other is behind, the result is like that of the right side;
for one situated behind, the left side is said to yield that same result.
This applies likewise to eating, sexual union, combat, and the gathering of fruits.
One should perform these rites when Vāyu is situated to the south;
however, a wise person should not undertake travel when Vāyu and Agni are in the north.
If one should travel out of delusion at such a time, even Brahmā does not return.
Travel is conducive to happiness when the earth element or the water element is predominant;
however, one should by all means never travel even when the ether element is predominant.
If, however, there is a reversal of the rising of the wind in the left and other zodiac signs, there will be agitation of the mind; because of that, the failure of one's undertakings occurs.
In the second house, the journey will indeed result in suffering;
in the fourth, there will be great loss; and in the fifth, there will be conflict with the directions.
In the sixth [year], there would be transgression; in the seventh, the onset of disease;
in the eighth, one should know death; and in the ninth, the destruction of the intellect.
In the tenth house there is bodily suffering; in the next, the loss of friends;
and during the midday meal, misfortune shall arise from all sides.
When there is a reversal of these zodiac signs and even of the positions of the elements,
one should know that all beings will be in fear and it will be unpleasant for the king.
By the power of the movement of the breath alone, the wise man should perform the examination of the auspicious and inauspicious day by day across all zodiac signs;
[the counts being] ten thousand, one thousand, and likewise six hundred.
The breaths of living beings enter and exit day after day;
fifteen such days constitute a fortnight, known as the first and the latter half.
From two of those [fortnights] one month arises, and two months become one season (ṛtu).

One should know that three seasons constitute one *ayana*, two such *ayanas* make a year (*samā*), and the lifespan is said to be one hundred years; however, this is reduced by the impairment of the breaths.
For as long as one remains in union with whichever [element], that is measured by its breaths;
by the power of the time of the breath alone, let the time of death be examined.
At the beginning of the year, when the sun is in the northern course (uttarāyaṇa).
Immediately after, the external wind flows for five nāḍīs in the south.
Then, if there are likewise five hundred [breaths] on the left,
and six *ghaṭikās* should remain for this life, it is declared that one will live for eighty years.
If one moves for seven *ghaṭikās*, one attains a lifespan of sixty-two years;
if one should move for eight *ghaṭikās*, one's [lifespan] is indicated as fifty years;
if one moves for nine *ghaṭikās*, the limit is thirty-three years.
It is taught that [the breath] flows through ten channels for twenty-eight years;
it flows through the left for half a day for twenty-five years.
If the wind flows during the day, one lives for twelve years;
if the wind flows for a full day and night, his life span is ten years.
If the wind flows for two days, one lives for eight years;
if the wind flows for three days, one lives for five years;
but if it should flow for four days, one lives for four years.
If the wind flows for five nights, his lifespan is three years.
If [the breath] moves for ten nights, the lifespan would be two years; if for a fortnight, it would be one year.
He whose [breath] flows for twenty days has six months of life remaining;
his lifespan from twenty-five days is three months.
(15) A lifespan of two months is proclaimed for twenty-six days;
or, with twenty-seven days on the left, one lives for one month.
In this [case], his lifespan is twenty-eight fortnights;
if there is one fortnight remaining here, his lifespan is ten days.
If it flows in the left for thirty days, he lives for five nights;
if for thirty-two days, his lifespan is proclaimed to be one day.
The life span shall be thirty-three days and thirty ghaṭikās;
this result occurs starting from the upward movement of the wind at the commencement of the solstice (ayana).
However, until the end of the period of the solstice, the portion [of the life span] remains only in the south.
As stated, beginning from all the transits, for five days the wind flows in the southern [channel] for one whose life lasts three years.
Starting from the solar transit (saṃkrānti) of the month of Caitra, for five days,
if the wind blows toward the south, that person will live for a maximum of eighteen years.
In the same way, for one whose vital wind flows through the left side,
various kinds of danger exist, other than death itself.
In whichever month it may be, at the beginning of the bright fortnight,
the wise man should then examine death by means of the movement of the breaths.
If the wind blows from the south for exactly one day and night, death will occur after three years;
if it blows for two days, death occurs within two years.
If Saumya (Mercury) flows thus, death occurs within three days; in the Dasa of Vatsara, death occurs within ten days; and in Māsa, death occurs within one month;
and in Eka, death occurs within one day.
Disease, loss of wealth, mental anguish, and conflict—
such are the results said to occur when the Sun and the Moon are both moving through the seventh house;
however, if the Sun or the Moon is situated in the seventh house during a fixed sign, [the results differ].
When the wind is situated there in the birth-constellation, it is called the Sāvitra-yoga;
if during this time the wind flows in one direction for half a day, [it is so].
If his death occurs at the age of fourteen, it is sufficient;
however, if he should sustain the Sāvitra Yoga for even a single day,
one should predict his death at the age of twelve.
When day and night have passed, that [life] perishes after ten years;
likewise, for one who has two days [remaining], his life lasts eight years.
Thus, for one who [sees it] for two days, his life is six years;
likewise, for one who [sees it] for four days, his lifespan is four years.
Thus, for one whose [wind] flows for five days, his life span is three years;
having begun the yoga in this manner, it likewise flows for ten days.
His lifespan is two and a half years plus thirty-six [days].
If, having thus commenced yoga, it should last for twelve days;
His life span is two years minus seventy-two days;
having begun the yoga in this manner, it lasts for fourteen days.
Including the fourth [day], his life span is one and a half years.
If death should occur at the end of the year [from the start] of such a five-day yoga,
and if one begins this very yoga and it flows for sixteen days,
then starting from that point, it should flow for seventeen days on one side alone.
If [the Moon] enters Yamāsya when the year is deficient by thirty-six days, death will certainly occur;
if it be nineteen [days], death will happen after eight months.
If it flows for twenty days, death will occur after six months;
if it flows for twenty-one days, death will occur after two months.
If the breath flows for twenty-nine days, his life will last ten days;
for one whose breath flows for thirty days, death will occur after five days;
and for one whose breath flows for thirty-one days, death will occur after three nights.
If [the breath] lasts for thirty-two days, death is declared to occur after three, two, or three days;
if it should last for thirty-three days, death will occur after one day.
If the wind should indeed blow from the left at the time of liberation,
it brings about the destruction of sons, friends, wife, wealth, livelihood, and kinsmen.
"Or likewise by other human signs, even external ones;
the discerning should indeed determine the proper and improper time. Thus ends the section on cows.
In the Kāśīkhaṇḍa:
"He who sits during the two twilights and combs his own hair until it becomes smoky shall indeed meet death within five days or three years."
If death should occur after four days, [the lifespan] is two years.
If death should occur after three days for one who has heard a sound when both ears were indeed covered by the hands, [that too is a sign]. For one year, death shall occur.
If there is no death within a year even though [the breath] remains inside the fire,
and if it exits simultaneously through both parts of its path,
or if the *brahmasūtra* is destroyed, then that [person] also perishes within a year.
If one suffers from sudden obesity and sudden physical ailments,
or if there is excessive anger or excessive disease, death will occur within a year;
likewise, if excrement, urine, and emaciation arise simultaneously.
In that month, on that lunar day, his death is imminent in that year,
if he should see a city of Gandharvas somewhere upon the top of a tree.
Even for him, death shall strike before the end of that year.
Or if one's own body becomes blackish-brown for no apparent reason,
it is proclaimed that his death will occur after one year.
If one's body is devoured by vultures, crows, jackals, donkeys, camels, and likewise by gayals, death shall come to him within a year.
Or if, even in a dream, one's afflicted body is devoured by these or by others, death will occur within a year; of this there is no doubt.
Whoever sees the sun fallen from the sky or the moon devoid of its radiance shall meet death before half a year has passed.
If one's lips and palate become dry and resemble the color of collyrium, his death will occur within half a year; of this there is no doubt.
If the moon is seen through the space between two fingers, one should observe that [person] for three finger-breadths; even such a person has a lifespan of half a year.
If one's own body becomes crooked or develops thousands of openings,
and these remain invisible [to others], death will occur within six months.
With limbs smeared with blood and fragrant unguents, he resembles a crow or a vulture;
abandoned by oil, extremely terrified, he wears no turban and is devoid of clothing.
His death shall occur before half a year passes; of this there is no doubt.
Furthermore, for one whose footprint appears broken in mud or in dust, [the same fate awaits].
One may see the sky moving as it takes on the form of a lizard,
yet one does not perceive the firefly when the two [eyes] are pressed by the fingers.
Or death will come to his eyes within half a year; of this there is no doubt.
[He sees] one who is black, short, holding an iron staff, and dressed in black attire.

If one sees such [omens] in a dream, death is certain within three months. If the sense organs do not perceive their respective objects, his death will occur at the end of a month; of this there is no doubt.
One's own head is ablaze with incoherent chatter that cannot be suppressed;
at night, one sees Indra’s bow and lightning even when there are no clouds, as if in a mirror.
One should observe a shadow, the appearance of a head, fire of a blue color,
or one who sees a peacock, as well as the mating of crows and swans.
Those who live for a month are subject to extreme cold and heat;
when one has bathed, there are apertures at the region of the heart, in the earth, the sun, and the moon.
But they declare that if one's shadow is absent, one has only half a month of life remaining.

If one experiences cold from the sun or heat from snow, or if one is devoid of luster, or if the complexion of the skin becomes yellow, death will occur within a fortnight; of this there is no doubt. Furthermore, if a sudden flame appears burning at the soles of the feet...
One born under Svāti does not see the bears or the Seven Sages;
half of his body is like that of a camel, and his vision is focused on a cool orb.
One who is discolored, whose garments are distorted, or who suddenly smells like a corpse upon his own body or becomes naked, perishes within seven nights.
In a dream, seeing a woman or oneself circumambulating [an object] to the right;
or seeing one's own food eaten by another; or seeing a bull as a vehicle.
Or if one should see another person carrying a staff, death will occur after three nights.
He who, at the time of eating, should see a woman with disheveled hair or naked, or one holding a noose, will also die immediately.
When one's own self is being consumed by the house, death will surely come to that person immediately; of this there is no doubt.
For mortals overcome by passion, that which appears red like blood is indeed death itself; it occurs immediately, without a doubt.
Thus, having understood the movement of time through external and internal signs,
one should indeed exert effort toward the supreme good after having examined it for that very duration.
Thus, having understood this well, the wise practitioner, established in the method of breath control (prāṇāyāma), should deceive the approaching time through the practice of yoga.
Thus ends the second chapter in the Compendium of the Yoga Śāstra.
Now, there are fifteen or ten channels; I shall describe the sequence of the winds:
Suṣumnā, Bhogadā, Hasti, Jihvā, Vṛṣā, and Yaśasvinī.
O Dear One, the principal vessels are said to be fifteen: Viśvodarā, Piṅgalā, Elā, Vāruṇī, Payasvinī, Alambuṣā, Kuhu, Gāndhārī, and Payasvinī, as well as Śaṅkhinī. Thus it is declared.
In the *Yogasāramañjarī*, in the *Bhāvopaniṣad*: Alambuṣā, Kuhū, Viśvodarī, Vāruṇā, Hastinī, Hāstijihvā, Yaśovatī,
Gāndhārī, Pūṣā, Śaṅkhinī, Sarasvatī, Ilā, and Piṅgalā.
Including Suṣumnā, there are fourteen channels;
however, in the Tāracintāmaṇi, fifteen channels are recorded.
Fourteen channels were proclaimed by Yājñavalkya;
sixteen channels are recorded as having been proclaimed by Candrajñāna.
Even according to the method of the measures of the zodiacal signs (*rāśimāna*),
as enjoined by Yājñavalkya in the *Sarvasāropaniṣad* and the *Yogasāramañjarī*: "Prāṇa, apāna, samāna, vyāna, and udāna."
And the Nāga, Kūrma, Kṛkara, Devadatta, and Dhanañjaya.
Vairaṃbha, Muktadāya, Prabhañjana, Samīraṇa, and Antaryāmī—these are said to be the fifteen great vital airs (mahāprāṇas). (p.
In the Bhāvopaniṣad:
Prāṇa, Apāna, Vyāna, Udāna, Samāna, Kūrma, Kṛkara, Devadatta, and Dhanañjaya.
In the *Praṇavacintāmaṇi*:
"O Beloved of the World, there are seventy-two thousand channels (*sirā*) in the body; through the flow of the vital air (*pavana*), these become thoroughly purified."
And in the Durikopaniṣad:
"There are seventy-two thousand channels within the range of the vital air. Thus says the Lord.
The body is said to consist of seventy-two thousand channels;
they depend upon the body just as a basket is held together by its binding cords.
In the *Yogasāramañjarī*:
From the root of the *śibhā* [lotus], moving upwards from the downward-facing [petals], there are thirty-two that go upwards;
some are long and some are short, and those that are short are spread everywhere.
In the Svādhiṣṭhāna, thousands of channels have arisen.
In Maṇipūra, two thousand channels are present in their contracted state;
in Anāhata, two thousand channels are perfectly manifested.
In the region of purity, one thousand channels are recorded as being closed;
ten thousand is the continuum of channels produced in the lotus of the command.
Ten thousand channels arise in the region of the head;
these veins, numbering sixty-four, extend upward like those originating from the *kanda*.
The seventy-two thousand secondary channels, having coiled around, are situated at the rear part of the middle body.
There are sixty-two principal channels for all embodied beings;
among them, fifteen vessels are remembered as the most important.
Īśvara said:
One channel extends outward, while another resides in the center of the heart;
through it, it receives nourishment, just as a field is fed by a canal.
Mathurā is gradually nourished by minerals produced from rasa.
The tongue named Gāndhārī, situated at the side as Piṅgalā,
is directed upward toward the aperture of Brahmā (brahmarandhra) and has emerged with many branches.
In the Churikopaniṣad: "Iḍā stands on the left, while Piṅgalā is on the right;
the channel situated at the side of Iḍā is called Hastijihvikā."
It has many branches and many trunks; from root to tip, it hangs with its face downward.
Together with Pūṣā and Alambuṣā, these two are known to extend upward along both sides;
branching out extensively, they reach as far as the fingertips.
And Yaśasvinī shall emerge from the big toe of Dakṣa;
this [channel] shall have many branches and be downward-facing from the *mūlādhāra*.
That great channel which is Śaṅkhinī is known to be upward-facing on the left.
It is held that [the body] extends from the divisions of the primary and secondary branches down to the tips of the toes;
and there is the channel called Kuhū, which is well-established both below and above.
Divided into many branches, Sarasvatī pervades and abides within the body; arising from its root, it is established as far as the tip of the tongue.
Both Jayā and Vijayā are born from the base of the navel;
they remain pervading the pair of eyebrows, the eyes, the tips of the ears, and the cheeks.
On either side of the Suṣumnā are born the Iḍā and the Piṅgalā;
they are situated within this body at the ends of the left and right nostrils.
Between those two is the supreme state; he who knows it is a knower of the Veda.
Within this body, which has a foundation of two finger-breadths, the vital winds arise.
For they always roam among the seventy-two thousand [beings].
Yājñavalkya says:
Within the body, know that the seat of fire has the luster of molten gold;
it is triangular for humans, and quadrangular with four feet.
"O beautiful one, know that the place of the moths at the edge of the mandala belongs to the winds, such as the vital breath (prāṇa) and the others. In the Uttara-gītā it is said:
'There are seventy-two thousand channels (nāḍīs) which are the domain of the winds.'"
In the *Yogasāramañjarī*: "Then, from the breath, it enters through both channels at a distance of twelve finger-breadths;
the movement upwards and downwards by means of the two leaders [the *iḍā* and *piṅgalā*] is said to constitute the day and night."
From the left and right channels, there arises that which is named the "seizer" (graha);
and those channels which are situated, completely enveloping this body.
O Goddess of the gods, the vital airs (vāyus) circulate within all of them;
among these, the principal one is Prāṇa, which is established below the kanda.
The vital breath (prāṇa) abides in these places as well: between the mouth and the nose, in the heart, in the kneecaps, and in the big toes of the feet.
The location of the apāna is said to be in the calves, the belly, and the region of the waist;
it resides in the hips, the ears, the middle of the eyes, the eyebrows, and the two fingers.
The Udāna wind resides at the joints and is also present in the feet and hands;
the Samāna wind, having pervaded the entire body, remains there at all times.
The five winds, beginning with Nāga, are situated within the skin, bones, and other tissues;
that which resembles a sapphire is proclaimed to be the form of Prāṇa.
Situated within the chest, this [vital energy] constantly fills these vital breaths (prāṇas).
Filled with inhalation and exhalation, and enveloped by the individual soul (jīva),
it is called "prāṇa" because it departs at the time of death.
Between the mouth and the nose, at the center of the eyebrows,
in the circle of the navel, in the big toe, and even in the nail, they call this the abode of the vital breath (prāṇa).
The water situated in the stomach and the essence (rasa) therein are made equal;
the vital breath (prāṇa) residing in the middle of the stomach does not make them separate from one another.
Ādinātha:
Furthermore, having placed water in the fire, one should place food and other offerings upon the water.
But he himself, having reached the apāna, moved with great speed along with it.
Thereupon, that fire situated within the center of the body proceeds toward the stomach;
then that radiance blazes throughout the entire middle of the body.
There, the fire, impelled by the vital breath (prāṇa-vāyu),
caused the water situated within the interior of the stomach to become exceedingly hot.
Then, having placed the food together with its condiments upon the water,
he caused it to be cooked by means of the fire-heated water.
Sweat and urine would become water; its potency (vīrya), form, and taste would become food and feces; thus the vital breath (prāṇa) would produce each separately.
This *apāna* wind carries away the food that has become impure, as well as semen, urine, and excrement; therefore, it is called *apāna*.
Resembling the wrath of Indra and appearing like a water-laden cloud,
he [fell] upon his penis, anus, thighs, eyes, and knees.
The Vyāna wind resides in the calves, the abdomen, the waist, and the root of the navel;
it is called Vyāna because it pervades the limbs and it excites the upward-moving breath (udāna).
Resembling great Jāmbūnada gold, it is the cause for the manifestation of activity;
it is located between the neck and the chest, at the waist, and also at the two ankles.
It also resides here unrestrained in the nose and the region of the buttocks;
it causes the lower lip and the face to quiver, and provokes the eyes and the lineage.
The vital air named Udāna causes actions to arise;
it possesses the color of lightning and fire, and it is the agent that produces the upward movement of breath. It resides in the feet, the hands, and also in the joints.
The vital air named Samāna brings together the limbs— whether they are yellowed, consumed, or smelled— and it consists of blood, bile, and phlegm.
Residing throughout the entire body, [the breath] has the appearance of white cow’s milk;
the upward-moving breath (udgāra) is called Nāga and resembles a dark blue cloud.
Kṛkara is hungry and resembles the Japā flower.

"Dhanañjaya resides in the *poṣa* [channel], having the color of great gold. Thus it is said in the *Praṇavacintāmaṇi*: "The two *nāgas*, Prāṇa and Apāna, have a color like the luster of *rājāvarta* stone;
the two *kūrmās*, Prāṇa and Apāna, are similar, having a luster like that of sapphire (*indranīla*)."
The *samāna* and *kṛkara* are like the sky and are auspicious to all;
the *śuddha* and *sphaṭika* resemble pure crystal and are equal; the *vyāna* and *anaṅgaja* are like the filaments of a lotus; while the *udāna* and *devadatta* are like the pollen of a lotus.
The two inner controllers, Nāga and Antaryāmin, are said to be pure and the color of lightning;
these two are the primary ones, possessing great vital force, and are the Vairambha and Prabhañjana winds.
Resembling dark-blue sapphire gems, they are proclaimed to have the form of wind. Having caused the two vital breaths (*prāṇa*) to ascend and pervading the body, one should move about.
Rising by means of the *samāna* breath, the *vāśinī* [nāḍī] effects firmness of the body;
rising by means of the inner controller (*antaryāmin*), the *alaṃbuṣā* attains the subtle body (*tanu*).
The winds named Piṅgalā, Pūṣan, Kūrma,
Hastijihvā, Devadatta, and Kṛkara are the vital breaths.
Yaśasvinī and Dhanañjayau, Suṣumnā and Prabhañjanau, Vairaṃbhā and Śaṅkhinī, and Sarasvatī with Muktivāyu.
Mounting the Mahāprāṇa, Viśvodarā proceeds forth.
The five winds beginning with Prāṇa are proclaimed to be male (puruṣa) in form;
the five winds beginning with Nāga are proclaimed to be female (strī) in form.
The five winds beginning with *dhanañjaya* are neuter;
however, the *apāna* wind is in the anus and is that which expels feces and urine.
The Samāna wind is at the navel and is the cause of hunger, thirst, and so forth;
the Udāna wind is in the region of the throat and is the cause of swallowing by the mind.
The Vyāna wind pervades all limbs and is supremely the producer of strength and voice;
the Nāga wind causes hiccups and belching, while the Kūrma wind causes the closing [of the eyes].
Kutkāra is Kṛkara, Devadatta is the one who causes yawning;
Dhanañjayasthālyakara is Vairaṃbha, the one who causes anger.
The inner controller, whose body consists of the five elements, acts as the purifier of liberation and brings about the knowledge of the phenomenal world within the body.

The Great Breath (mahāprāṇa), like the wind that shatters all things, swiftly brings about the abandonment of the body through knowledge, dispassion, and higher realization (vijñāna). Thus, one who knows the true nature of the vital breaths should practice yoga.
Thus ends the third chapter, titled "The Description of the Vital Channels," in the Yogaśāstra.
Breath control.
Agastya:
Whatever action one whose self is purified by breath-control (prāṇāyāma) performs,
that indeed bears fruit without doubt, whether done with great effort or otherwise.
For one who lacks breath control (prāṇāyāma), recitation, fire-offerings, worship, and so forth [are fruitless].
All that is performed with effort does not bear fruit at all if it is done without breath-control (prāṇāyāma); such action is rendered useless.
Therefore, those who desire auspiciousness should practice breath control with diligent effort.
In the *Amṛtabindu Upaniṣad*:
"Just as the sins of those who travel to the mountains are burned away by the power of Yama’s messengers,
so too are the defects produced by the senses burned away by the restraint of the vital breath (*prāṇa*)."
In the *Yogasāramañjarī*: "Neither during indigestion, nor when there is an acid eructation, nor while suppressing feces or urine;
nor during vomiting, nor during dysentery, nor when excessively possessed by spirits."
Nor should one perform it toward a worthy person or a preceptor while afflicted by hunger or thirst.
One should not perform breath control (prāṇāyāma); if one should do so, one will become subject to disease.
Gorakṣa says:
Just as those seeking water do not drink it immediately from machines, conduits, and the like, but rather slowly, so too the yogi, free from fatigue, should gradually [draw] the vital air.
In the *Dhyānanādabindūpaniṣad*: "Just as a man might draw up water by means of a lotus stalk, even so the yogi established in the state of yoga should draw up the vital air."
In the *Yogasāramañjarī*: One should increase the measure by one *mātrā* and even half a *mātrā* day by day;
whatever becomes easy to perform, having abandoned that, one should proceed further.
In the *Vāsiṣṭha*:
"Just as a lordly elephant in the forest, though being restrained by men, might destroy them through lack of restraint, so too does the vital breath [destroy] through lack of awareness."
And just as that very elephant is gradually tamed through training, so too is he.
It becomes free from defects over time, gentle, and diminishes;
thus, through practice, it gradually reaches the state of cessation.
He who maintains [the mind] within the body by his own will and does not allow it to commit any fault is like an elephant urged forward that destroys the enemy army;
mounted upon it with strength, he protects the rider.
"Likewise, the vital breath (prāṇa), firmly established in the body and properly impelled, destroys all sins and protects that very body.
Thus it is said in the Sūta Saṃhitā: "Having thoroughly understood everything, beginning with the equinoxal transit (viṣu-saṃkrānti)..."
Having practiced the southern course and performed the eclipse-observance during the northern course,
and likewise having honored the [deceased] with the offering of food while avoiding the tearing apart [of the body],
one who relies upon the state of being a mourner or the state of birth-impurity becomes pure day by day.
Having understood this, one should constantly practice *kumbhaka* like a full jar;
at the time of the *sandhyā*, the wise man should perform it except during periods of birth or death impurity (*sūtaka* and *pretaka*).
One should never fail to perform it throughout the day and night, even during all six *sandhyā* periods.
One should practice *kumbhaka* with great effort until it becomes full;
if one recites [the mantra] during the birth-impurity (*sūtaka*) or the death-impurity (*pretaka*), it shall become fruitless.
Therefore, with every effort, one should practice thoroughly among those who have been purified.
When the vital breath (prāṇa) has entered equally into the place of Piṅgalā within the Iḍā,
that is called "the eclipse of the moon" by the best among the knowers of reality.
When the vital breath (prāṇa) reaches the location of Kuṇḍalinī by means of Piṅgalā,
that is called a solar eclipse by the best among the knowers of reality.
The transition from both Piṅgalā and Iḍā is declared to be the northern course (uttarāyaṇa); such is the Vedic revelation regarding Piṅgalā.
The non-transference of the vital breath (vāyu) into the iḍā and the piṅgalā is declared by the sages who have reached the further shore of the Vedas to be the southern course (dakṣiṇāyana).
When the vital breath reaches the junction of the iḍā and piṅgalā [nādīs], [that is the moment].
O best among those who know the body, that is then declared to be a year within the body.
O best of scholars, when the vital breath (prāṇa) has entered the mūlādhāra,
that is declared by the ascetics, the best of ascetics, to be the first equinox (viṣuva).
When [the breath] enters the head of the best of sages, which is designated as *prāṇa*,
that is declared by the righteous who contemplate reality to be the other *viṣuva*.
"Exhalation and inhalation—this entire process constitutes the transition between the months.
Thus says Dattātreya: "Having slightly expelled [the breath], one should contract [it]; again in that same way, and again likewise."
The wise have declared this previously as *śarīra* (the body);
they know that the state of being a corpse (*pretakatva*) or the state of birth-impurity (*sūtakatva*) pertains to the left and right [channels].

The six junctions (*ṣaṭsandhi*). Earth, water, fire, air, space, and so forth constitute five junctions; when combined with the end of exhalation (*recaka*) and the beginning of inhalation (*pūraka*), they become six. Their essential natures have been explained previously.
Parāśara says: "Having contracted the middle [fingers], [one joins] the two index fingers with the thumb, ring finger, and so forth."

The wise man, having firmly closed the nostrils with his fingers as prescribed in the *Amṛtabindu* and *Uṣan* Upaniṣads, should, being self-controlled, slowly inhale the air through one nostril for the sake of attaining yoga, exactly as it has been taught.
The binding of the nostrils with the little finger, the ring finger, and the thumb.
That should be known as prāṇāyāma, performed firmly without the two index fingers.
Śiva and Vyāsa:
Pressing the tip of the nose with the five fingers, accompanied by the Praṇava.
This mudrā, which destroys all sins, belongs to both forest-dwellers and householders;
it is formed by pressing one nostril with a finger while holding the other with the other hand.
One should expel the abdominal air; this is declared to be *recaka*.
O auspicious one, one should fill the body with external air, like a vessel being held steady.
It is called *pūraka* because of filling; likewise, they know it as *kumbhaka*.
Mārkaṇḍeya said:
Prāṇāyāma is traditionally defined as the complete restraint of the vital breaths.
Patañjali: Prāṇāyāma is the cessation of the movement of exhalation and inhalation.
Vyāsa says: Inhalation is the drawing in of external air;
exhalation is the emission of the air from the internal cavity.
The cessation of the movement of those two is *prāṇāyāma*.
It is of four kinds: *saṃvartaka*, *sadhūma*, *vidhūma*, *sagarbha*, and *vigarbhaka*.
Prāṇāyāma is sixfold, consisting of both *lakṣya* (with an object) and *vilakṣya* (without an object).
Prāṇāyāma performed with breath alone is "with smoke" (*sadhumā*). It is "without smoke" (*vidhumā*) when performed with the two syllables of the *haṃsa*, or with the *praṇava*.
The "pregnant" [kumbhaka] occurs through the contemplation of the nature of the *haṃsa* or through the contemplation of the nature of the *praṇava*.
It is "with seed" (*sagarbha*) when preceded by meditation on the deity of the mantra. In the case of the simple *kumbhaka*, it occurs within the *suṣumnā*.
"The restraint of the vital breath (prāṇa) alone is the 'with-mark' (salakṣya); the mere desire to enter the suṣumnā is the 'without-mark' (vilakṣya). Thus it is said. In the Āditya Purāṇa:
"Exhalation (recaka), the void (śūnyaka), inhalation (pūraka), and likewise retention (kumbhaka)..."
Thus, the wise have declared that prāṇāyāma here is of four kinds.
In the *Amṛtanādabindūpaniṣad*:
"Having drawn up the breath into space and made it void, being selfless, one should unite with the state of voidness; this is the definition of exhalation (*recaka*)."
Śrī Dakṣiṇāmūrti:
First, the wise one should fill [the breath] through the left nostril;
thereafter, he should meditate upon the mantra there eleven times.
Thereafter, one should recite the praise of the Lord ten times with that very same [mantra].
One should mutter the mantra nine times and accomplish the practice in this very manner. Thus it is said:
"The wise man should slowly exhale the abdominal air through the *piṅgalā* four times, and then fill [the lungs] slowly and gently through the *iḍā* for half that duration."
"The wise one should thus again perform purgation and again fill [the body] in this manner. Thus it is said in the *Yogasāramañjarī*:
"Having filled [it] through the left channel, one should release [the air] outward through the right."
Again, filling with the right [nostril], one should exhale many times through the left;
in this manner, there are hundreds upon hundreds of *kumbhaka* breath-retentions for the purified channels.
"One should perform [the practice] with the *haṃsa* [mantra], standing within the *barhis* [grass]. Thus says Dattātreya:
"The exhalation (*recaka*) is properly prescribed to be twice the duration of the inhalation (*pūraka*)."
"The time for the retention (kumbhaka) is praised as being twice that of the exhalation (recaka).
Thus says Pārāśara:
"Having filled the iḍā with sixteen [counts], one should fill it with sixty-four."
One should exhale through the solar channel (sūryanāḍī) thirty-two times and practice with the syllable *praṇava*.
In the *Yogasāramañjarī*:
"The minor [recitation] consists of twelve mātrās; the middling is said to be double that;
and the superior is declared to be triple, consisting of thirty-six tāla-mātrās."
Viśvāmitra says: Having uttered [the mantra] three times during inhalation (pūraka), four times during retention (kumbhaka),
and three times during exhalation (recaka), the practice of breath control (prāṇāyāma) is prescribed.
In the *Praṇavacintāmaṇi*:
"One should place the syllable *A* during inhalation (*pūraka*), and the syllable *U* during retention (*kumbhaka*);
likewise, one should place the syllable *M* during exhalation (*recaka*). In this manner, the *Nāda* (the primordial sound) is praised through meditation. Thus it is said.

Having filled [the breath] with the mantra "haṃsa, haṃsa," one should perform the retention (kumbhaka) with the seed-syllable "so'haṃ"; one should exhale with the "haṃsa" mantra—this is the definition of prāṇāyāma.
Yājñavalkya:
One should recite the Gāyatrī, together with the Vyāhṛtis, the Praṇava, and the Śiras, three times while restraining the breath; that is called Prāṇāyāma.
Bhāradvāja says:

One should recite the Gāyatrī twelve times, preceded by the seven vyāhṛtis, with the Praṇava at the beginning and end, and accompanied by the heart-mantra (hṛdaya); this is one breath-restraint (prāṇasaṃyama).
This breath control (prāṇāyāma) has been prescribed for the twice-born who is incapable [of other means].
But for a child and for others, the first-mentioned [method] is recommended.
Viśvāmitra says:
Seated properly upon the seat, one should fill the abdomen with the left [nostril],
perform three cycles by means of retention (kumbhaka), and then exhale through the right.

Yājñavalkya says: The twelfth *oṃkāra* is for filling (*pūraṇa*), the sixteenth *dhruva-oṃkāra* is for retention (*kumbhaka*), and ten *oṃkāras* are for exhalation (*recaka*); that is called *prāṇāyāma*.
The superior [type] is said to be ninefold, while the middling is according to the number of seasons.

They say that the first three [types of breath control] are inferior; however, in the practice of *prāṇāyāma*, one should first rely upon *kumbhaka* (retention), which is devoid of exhalation (*recaka*) and inhalation (*pūraka*).
Indeed, *prāṇāyāma* as *kumbhaka* consists of the recitation beginning with the *vyāhṛtis* and ending with the *Śiras*.
Bharadvāja says:
Prāṇāyāma performed daily for sixteen times, accompanied by the Vyāhṛtis and the Praṇava,
purifies even the killer of a learned Brāhmaṇa within a month.
Bṛhaspati and Saṃvarta state: "Whatever sin has been committed mentally, verbally, or through physical actions and the like—
all that is swiftly destroyed when three breath-restraints (prāṇāyāmas) are performed."
Through inhalation (pūraka) one attains union with Viṣṇu; through retention (kumbhaka), one reaches the presence of Brahmā.
By means of the third, the exhaling breath (recaka), one may attain the state of the Lord.
In the *Yogasāramañjarī*:
Pūraka is Brahmā, Kumbhaka is said to be Viṣṇu,
Recaka is Rudra, and Trāṭaka is Nirañjana.
That which is joined with short, long, and protracted [breaths], along with exhalation (recaka), inhalation (pūraka), and retention (kumbhaka),
and is performed exactly as described, is called prāṇāyāma.
A practitioner should perform breath control (prāṇāyāma) with effort, using either the three-syllable mantra beginning with "A," the Haṃsa-mantra, or the Praṇava (Oṃ).
Bṛhaspati:

Having assumed the bound posture (baddhāsana), having restrained the vital breaths (prāṇas), and having again recollected the Ṛṣis and so forth, one should practice breath control (prāṇāyāma) while remaining silent with eyes closed.
In the *Yogasāramañjarī*:
"The lunar maṇḍala is circular, pervaded by the drop (bindu), the individual soul (jīva), and water;
the fiery maṇḍala is triangular, pervaded by the drop, the vital breath (prāṇa), and air."

The *bindu*, the *praṇava*, the *jīva*, and the letter *sa* [constitute] water; the letter *va* is water. That which is pervaded by these is to be known as the circular lunar orb and the *iḍā* channel.
The *bindu*, the *praṇava*, the *prāṇa*, the letter *ya*, and the letter *ra* are fire; that which is pervaded by these is the triangular fire.
The mandala should be understood as the piṅgalā nāḍī.
The bindu, conjoined with consciousness, is circular like the solar mandala;
it is circular and conjoined with the bindu, the praṇava, consciousness, and the syllable hrīṃ.
The solar disc is to be known as the suṣumnā channel.
Having thus understood the true nature of the channels (nāḍīs), one should begin the practice of inhalation (pūraka) and so forth.
This is the intended meaning:
One should fill [the breath] with "Oṃ Saṃ Vaṃ. One should retain it with "Oṃ Saṃ Hrīṃ. One should exhale with "Oṃ Yaṃ Raṃ.
Having filled [it] through the left channel (nāḍī), one should release it externally through the right;
having again filled [it] through the right, one should discard it many times through the left.
In this manner, there are one hundred kumbhakas for each of the purified channels.
Abiding within by means of the innate *haṃsa* which is most exalted,
he beholds the world strewn with the atoms of radiant energies.
In the *Praṇavacintāmaṇi*:
"One should practice the breath in succession through both the left and right pathways."
Every day, according to the rule, at the four proper times.
Or for three or four years, or even for three or four months.
"If a king among yogis practices for six years or even six months,
he attains the purification of the channels (*nāḍī-śuddhi*), characterized by distinct signs.
Thus it is said in the *Yogasāramañjarī*.
Lightness, health, freedom from greed, a slight clarity, intense luster,
an increase in the digestive fire, and leanness [arise] in the noble one.
And it necessarily extends the clarity of the sound.
In Haṭhayoga:
at the end of pūraka, the bandha named Jālandhara should be performed;
at the end of kumbhaka and at the beginning of recaka, the Uḍḍiyāṇa should be performed.
Sūryabheda, Ujjāyī, as well as Cītkāra, Śītalī, Bhastrikā,
Bhramarī, Mūrchā, and Kumbhaka— thus [prāṇāyāma] is of eight types.

She is called *Sūryabhedanī* because, through retention (*kumbhaka*), she pierces the solar orb situated within the *suṣumnā*. She is called *Manujjananī* because, by means of retention, she generates the mantra in the form of the *praṇava* below.
Having restrained the vital breaths in the *apāna* and performing the lock (*bandha*) at the throat,
by means of which [the yogis] give birth to the stars— that is the *kumbhaka*.

This *tāra* emits the phonemes with a whistling sound; by means of it, the *kumbhaka* [retention] occurs, through which a shower of nectar is made to flow from the moon into all the channels (*nāḍīs*).
That which is called Śītalī is the destroyer of the phenomena of suffering by that very means.
Just as the air from a bellows burns away the impurities of metals,
so too, because it burns away sins, it is designated as "Bhastrikā" (the Bellows).
Or it is called *bhastrikā* because it sustains the vital breath (*prāṇa*) like a bellows;
*bhrāmarī* is said to be [the practice of] whirling and so forth, according to its various respective locations.
That which is called *kumbhaka* bestows the fruit of all accomplishments according to the sages;
because by it the vital air becomes motionless (*mūrchā*), it is therefore sung as *mūrchita*.

Kumbhaka is that which consists of the retention of breath, having abandoned both exhalation (recaka) and inhalation (pūraka), as it was previously practiced by the masters of yoga and the wise sages.
Having stated that "this is prāṇāyāma," that indeed is the *kevala-kumbhaka* (isolated retention).
That which one performs after exhaling and filling [the breath] is indeed the *saṃhita-kumbhaka* (combined retention).
One should properly practice either the *saṃhita* or the *kumbhaka* breath control;
one should fill the air through the throat and exhale it through the throat-passage.
This is the bhujaṅgī-karaṇa; kumbhaka is remembered as being of nine kinds.
When the air situated within moves outward, that is [the first].
In that very state, the complete cessation [of breath] is declared to be external *kumbhaka*;
it occurs when the external air, having entered the belly, is completely restrained.
Immediately following that, the best among those who know yoga have described the *kumbhaka*.

When the movement [of the breath] within the circle at the tip of the nose has ceased by means of the exhalation (*praśvāsa*), and the wind has dissolved— that is called the external *kumbhaka* by those who know it.
Patañjali [states] in the Vyāsabhāṣya: "Where there is an absence of movement preceded by inhalation (śvāsa), that is external breath control (prāṇāyāma);
where there is an absence of movement preceded by exhalation (praśvāsa), that is internal."
The third is the stalk-function (*staṃbha-vṁtti*). The region between the two nostrils is called the "stalk" (*staṃba*).
The stalk-function is that which is situated within the stalk. It is that state wherein the internal state arises at once through a single effort;
and without exhalation, the breath dissolves into the tip of the nose.
Then, the "post-like" mode of functioning is to be known; this is the third [type], the kumbhaka.
In the third *kumbhaka*, just as water placed upon a heated stone undergoes contraction on all sides,
so too there is an absence of movement in both [the breaths] simultaneously.
The restraint of the vital breath (prāṇāyāma) is declared by the most eminent knowers of Yoga to be threefold, according to the distinction of time: namely, superior, middling, and inferior.
Six hundred and three thousand measures constitute a heavy *kumbhaka*;
half of that is declared to be medium, and half of that is remembered as inferior.
According to the divisions of fortnight, month, and year, their names are proclaimed by the yogis as "long," "subtle," and "extremely subtle" in the characteristics of the perfected ones.
In the *Yogavācaspatya*:
"Indeed, this [cognition], having been practiced through repeated cognition, proceeds by way of years, months, fortnights, and so forth;
it clearly perceives the spatial and temporal dimensions, numbers, and its own knee-joints when touched by the hand."
