The first upward movement (udghāta) is slow, measured by three thousand six hundred intervals (mātrās) consisting of discrete time-units;
likewise, when doubled, it becomes the second, which is medium.
Thus, when tripled, the third is called "intense" (tīvra).

Having performed exhalation and inhalation, firmly binding the breath and forcefully obstructing it at the opening of the Brahma-door, the disciplined practitioner should remain mindful of both the external and internal [breath].
Devoted to breath control (prāṇāyāma), one should practice this pure kumbhaka three times every day; this wealth, guarded by the lords of yogis, is difficult to attain.
Having blocked the channel at the root of the *nāḍī* by means of the path of the breath, one remains in a state of bliss or non-bliss while restraining the fire;
thereafter, with eyes fixed on the heart in the upper part of the head, that is called *kumbhaka*, which awakens the inner sound (*nāda*).
Just as one with focused intellect, having restrained the breath, gradually releases it through the *piṅgalā* [nāḍī],
so should one practice separately that which is called *recaka*, like water flowing from a clay pot with an extremely fine crack.
Dattātreya said: In the heart, at the location of the head, between the eyebrows, and in the region of the navel—
wherever death has entered the vital breath, become intent upon its restraint.
Ādinātha:

As long as the activity of the mind exists there, so long does the activity of the vital breath exist; for with the destruction of one, the other ceases, and from the activity of one, the activity of the other arises.
When the two paths are obstructed, the function of the group of senses ceases, and there is the attainment of the state of the path;
even then, the destruction of the vital breath (pavana) cannot be accomplished by the practice of the six-limbed yoga and other such means.
The destruction of the mind, however, is indeed easily accomplished in a mere moment through the grace of the Guru.
Therefore, let those who would destroy the mind [know that] by the destruction of mental activity, the wind is destroyed first.
On this point there is a scriptural text:

"Just as a bird tied by a string, having flown in every direction and finding no resting place elsewhere, settles down at its very bond; for the mind, my dear, is tied to the vital breath (prāṇa). Thus, the mind itself is the individual soul (jīva).
In the *Yogavāsiṣṭha*:
"For it is because of the mind that one is called a living being (*jīva*).
In the *Jñānasāra*:
The tip of the nose, the navel, and the heart as the third—
these are the locations for the individual soul (jīva) established by Śiva.

Regarding this, there is a scriptural passage (śruti): "One should know that the waking state resides in the palate; one should indicate that dreaming resides in the throat; deep sleep resides in the heart; and the fourth state (turya) is situated in the head."
Having thus understood both wind and life-force, and having restrained the mind within the heart,
one should perform the restraint of the vital breaths, like a lion for the elephant of death.
The nature of sound (nāda) is described in the context of the yoga of dissolution (layayoga).
Thus ends the fourth chapter, titled "The Nature of Prāṇāyāma," in the Compendium of Yoga Śāstra.

Now, regarding withdrawal (*pratyāhāra*): in the *Śivayoga*, it is said that withdrawal is simply the cessation of this mind—which has arisen as a vast ocean of unimpeded waves of consciousness turned inward—along with its various and manifold transformations; that is, the swallowing up of those various modifications. Thus it is described.
By those who know yoga.
That indeed is withdrawal (pratyāhāra); with a steady and joyful mind, I always worship Him.
In the Sūtasamhitā: "Now, O great sage, I shall explain withdrawal (pratyāhāra)."
The sense-faculties wander within the hearts by their very nature.
The withdrawal of those [senses] by force is called pratyāhāra;
being concentrated, one should perceive everything that one sees as Brahman.
This is what is called *pratyāhāra*, as previously taught by the knowers of Brahman:
whatever one does until the end of life, whether pure or impure.
One should offer all that to Brahman; this is called withdrawal (pratyāhāra).
Alternatively, one should perform the obligatory rites with the intention of worshipping Brahman, and likewise perform those rites for specific desires; that is called withdrawal (pratyāhāra).
Alternatively, having drawn in the breath, one should restrain it in various locations:
the wind at the root of the teeth, then at the ear, and from the throat to the chest;
drawing it from the region of the chest, one should restrain it in the bulb of the navel.
Having drawn [the breath] from the navel-center (nābhikanda), one should restrain it within Kuṇḍalī;
the wise man should restrain Kuṇḍalī at its location in the Mūlādhāra.
Likewise, one should restrain [the breath] at the anus, the two hips, the middle of the two thighs,
and from there at the two knees, the two shanks, and the big toes.
This is called withdrawal (pratyāhāra), which is always practiced by those devoted to withdrawal;
such is the case for the high-souled person who is thus engaged in practice.
O observer of noble vows, all sins and the disease of worldly existence are destroyed;
or else, O sage, I shall describe another form of withdrawal (pratyāhāra) to you.
Drawing the breath through both nostrils while remaining motionless in the svastika posture,
the wise practitioner should fill the air from the soles of the feet to the crown of the head.
Afterwards, likewise in the two feet, and similarly in the *mūlādhāra*,
in the *nābhikanda*, in the center of the heart, in the throat, and at the root of the palate.
One should fix [the mind] between the eyebrows, on the forehead, and likewise on the crown of the head, while recollecting the five-syllable mantra of Śiva: A-KĀ-RO-U-KĀ-RA-MĀ-ŚCA.
One should mutter "Aiṃ"; thus the vital breath is restrained, for that indeed is Pratyāhāra.
Or else, O tiger among sages, I shall describe Pratyāhāra to you:
the wise man, being composed, draws back the notion of the Self from the body.
One should dissolve [the mind] in the non-conceptual state where there is no duality between self and non-self;
this is declared by those who truly know the Vedānta as *pratyāhāra* (withdrawal).

Because the restraint of the vital breath (*prāṇa*) must be preceded by knowledge of the vital points (*marmans*), the locations where I reside are now described— from the aperture of Brahmā (*brahmarandhra*) down to the tips of the nails.
Śrīdatta states in the *Śārīra*:
Know that the distance between the knee and the foot is twelve finger-breadths (aṅgulas) each;
one should likewise specify the distance from the knee up to the navel as being exactly the same.
Know that from the navel to the heart is twelve finger-breadths (aṅgulas) doubled;
likewise, from the heart to the aperture of Brahmā (brahmarandhra) is twelve finger-breadths doubled.
Having understood this, one should hold the breath according to the measure of each successive finger-breadth:
at the nine gates, at the end of the throat, in the center of the heart, and in the center of the navel.
Then, from the base, middle, and tip of the hands, [the breath reaches] the aperture of the Brahma-randhra.
The two knees, the tips of the knees, and the two roots of the thighs—
O Daughter of the Mountain, these are said to be the twenty-five joints.
In the *Yogasāramañjarī*:
the two hands, the two arms, and beyond that the two feet;
then the two thighs, the calves, the two big toes, and the pair of knees.
The collarbone, the elbow, the base of the neck, and the two shoulders;
then the tip of the uvula, the nose, the middle of the eyebrows, and the crown of the head.
The tip of the forehead, the tip of the *suṣumnā*, and beyond that the *dvādaśānta*;
these are among the twenty-eight vital points (*marmas*) located at the end of the *dvādaśānta* for those who are liberated.
Day by day, in ninety-six locations, a man should duly fix his vital breath (prāṇa) for one ghaṭikā, bringing it there and then withdrawing it again;
thus he should practice for six months in the twenty-five junctions (sandhis).
Having fixed the vital breath for one muhūrta at a time and drawing it back again,
the knower of yoga, after practicing this for three seasons, then [proceeds] to the eight limbs.
One should practice diligently for six months, directing the breath for five *ghaṭikās* at a time into each of the locations of the five elements individually; then,
one should again practice diligently for six months, directing it into the locations up to the *dvādaśānta*.
Likewise, in the twelve locations, he should repeatedly draw in and then release the breath for one *muhūrta* each within the internal eight *nāḍīs*,
while focusing his undistracted mind on the meditation of the deities residing therein.
Thus, the yogi who practices the six-fold dhāraṇā should diligently practice pratyāhāra for a year,
gradually by means of kumbhaka.
Having attained the perfection of yoga, one then becomes identical with the essence of all reality (tattvas).
Furthermore, one gains atomicity, magnitude, and the power of hearing from afar; the ability to assume any form at will, the speed of thought, and the power of entering the bodies of others.
Death at one's own will, the sight of sporting with the gods,
the fulfillment of desired intentions, and always unimpeded movement.
Knowledge of the three times, freedom from the pairs of opposites, superknowledge of the thoughts of others and so forth,
and the power to paralyze the sun, wind, fire, and water.
"O fair-faced one, these characteristics can be attained in this manner.
Thus, it is said in the *Praṇavacintāmaṇi*.
All the vital points (marmasthāna) within the body pertain to both yoga and liberation.
I shall describe all of them exactly as they are known:
the two big toes, the two ankles, and the middle of the two thighs.
O Girijā, the anus is at the rear, and in the middle of the body is the penis;
then the navel, the heart, and the unsurpassed pit of the throat.
The root of the palate, the nose, the circle at the base of the eyes,
the middle of the eyebrows, the forehead, and the crown of the head— all these are worshipped by all the gods.
Listen now to the individual measurements for all the vital points (marmas):
the foot and the ankle measure four and a half finger-breadths.
The middle part of the foot and the ankle should be known as one finger-breadth (aṅgula);
the middle of the shank and the base of the altar (citi) are eleven finger-breadths.
O Śivā, two finger-breadths below the root of the navel is the [perineum];
from the tip of the heart to the base of the thigh is four and a half finger-breadths;
and the base of the thigh is said to be ten finger-breadths above the knees, O beloved of the world.
From the middle of the thighs, the root of the anus is nine finger-breadths away;
it is likewise declared to be the center of the body, while the base of the anus itself is two finger-breadths [from that].
O lotus-faced one, from the navel to the midpoint between the eyebrows is fourteen finger-breadths;
from the center of the heart to the pit of the throat is six finger-breadths beyond that.
From the pit of the throat to the root of the tongue is four finger-breadths;
from the location of the eyes to the root of the tongue is four and a half finger-breadths.
Therefore, know that the distance between one's own eyebrows is half a finger-breadth;
the place called the forehead (lalāṭa) should be three finger-breadths above the midpoint of the eyebrows.
From the forehead to the aperture of space (brahmarandhra), there is a distance of three finger-breadths for oneself;
having mentally ascended the vital air (vāyu) to these locations, one should hold it there.
Thus, for the sake of attaining yoga, the wise person should daily practice in this manner at the twenty-five joints and also in the vital points (*marmasthāna*).
For one who performs breath control (prāṇāyāma) by drawing [the breath] from place to place,
all passions perish and his yoga becomes perfected.
In the *Praṇavacintāmaṇi*:
"O Pārvatī, there is a specific method of withdrawal (*pratyāhāra*) regarding these locations;
I shall explain that withdrawal according to the procedure of the order of emanation."
The wise one, knowing the locations, draws the vital air from one place to another.
But he who thus maintains [the practice] in two ways, both in reverse and in direct order, [attains success].
Freed from all diseases, one shall live as long as the moon and stars endure.
From the *Yogasāramañjarī*:
Having drawn in the breath with a full *kumbhaka*, [one should hold it] between the thumb and the top of the head.
One should hold the breath with the intellect and impel the practice of prāṇāyāma.
Having drawn [the breath] from the aperture of the sky (the crown of the head), one should hold it at the forehead;
then, having drawn the wind from the forehead, one should restrain it between the eyebrows.
Drawing [the breath] from the base of the eyebrows, one should restrain it in the middle of the eyes;
drawing the vital breath (prāṇa) from the eyes, one should restrain it at the base of the channel (nālā).
Drawing [the breath] upward from the base of the nose, one should restrain it at the root of the tongue;
drawing it upward from the root of the tongue, one should restrain it in the pit of the throat.
From the pit of the throat to the center of the heart, from the center of the heart to the center of the navel;
from the center of the navel again to the penis, from the penis to the foundation-circle (ādhāramaṇḍala);
from the middle of the body to the anus, O Gaurī, and from the anus to the root of the perineum (vāśepha).
One should restrain it from the base of their thighs into the space between them;
from there, one should restrain it into the knees; and from the base of the knees into the two hips, one should restrain it into the root of those.
Again, from that root of the *citi*, likewise from the middle of the two calves,
having drawn [the breath] up from the base of the calves, one should restrain it at the ankle of the foot.
Having drawn [the breath] properly with both heels, one should restrain it at the tips of the big toes;
thus, having drawn the vital air from its place, the wise knower of yoga who maintains it with his intellect in both reverse and forward order—
Freed from all diseases, the wise man shall live as long as the moon and stars,
having drawn the vital air through the two channels into the sides of the Kuṇḍalinī.
O Girijā, he who can hold [the breath] simultaneously becomes a possessor of yogic perfection;
having raised the vital air as before, he should hold it within the void at the center of the heart.
Before long, he attains yoga and shall go to the state of the Supreme Self.
Drawing the breath through both nostrils, he should fill his belly for a long time.
Having fixed [the gaze] between the eyebrows and behind the eyes with a concentrated mind, one should maintain it for even a moment; such a person attains the supreme goal.
One should retain [the breath] for five *ghaṭīs* each upon the five elements; there will be mastery over each respective element for him, without a doubt.
Likewise, one should retain it for their corresponding measures as the cause of accomplishment.
Thus indeed should the best of yogis maintain the fivefold Brahman.
The body, for its part, is thus composed of the five elements by its very nature;
likewise, it is always said by you to consist of wind, bile, and phlegm.
For all those of a windy temperament whose minds are attached to yogic practices,
the body certainly withers away through the mere restraint of the vital breath.
If one possesses a *pitta*-dominant constitution, the body does not wither away for long;
however, for those of a *kapha*-dominant constitution, the body becomes full very quickly.
When that orb of the earth has declined, the bodies of embodied beings undergo graying,
just as grasses in water gradually turn white.
When the fire element wanes, hunger and thirst perish, as does the vital air;
when the air element wanes, one constantly lives by means of space alone.
"Thus, upon the dissolution of each respective [element], there is death; life is the sustaining of the elements.
In five hundred years, or a hundred thousand, death shall not otherwise occur. Thus it is stated in the *Amṛtanādabindu Upaniṣad*.
Having contemplated the mind as the formulator of intentions, the wise man withdraws it into the self;
thus holding the self steady is proclaimed as *dhāraṇā*.
In the Sūta-saṃhitā:
"Now, O observer of the fivefold vows, I shall explain that [meditation]:
one should fix the external space within the void situated in the center of the body."
In the vital breath, one should likewise [dissolve] the external air; in the fire, the internal fire;
in the water-element, the water; and in the earth-portion, the earth, O great sage.
O Sage, while reciting the mantra known as Hayarāvalakāra, the intended meaning is this:
from the Self (Ātman) arose space (ākāśa); from space, air (vāyu); from air, fire (agni); from fire, water (āpaḥ).

"From water, earth. Thus, one should place the respective seed-syllables in sequence: from the *brahmarandhra* to the middle of the eyebrows; from the middle of the eyebrows to the heart; from the heart to the navel; from the navel to the knees; and from the knees to the feet.
This dhāraṇī, which purifies all sins, has been proclaimed by me.
The portion of the earth up to the knees is said to be the drinking vessel of the waters.
From the anus to the end of the heart is called the fire-mandala;
from the heart to the end of the eyebrows is called the wind-mandala.
Likewise, the portion of space is proclaimed to extend up to the head of the Prājña;
Brahmā is situated in the portion of earth, and Viṣṇu likewise in the portion of water.
Likewise, one should meditate on Īśāna in the fire portion, Īśvara in the air portion,
and the highly wise Sadāśiva in the space portion.
Alternatively, O bull among sages, I shall tell you the method of retention (dhāraṇā).
One should contemplate the Moon in the mind, Śiva in the direction [of space], Viṣṇu in the ear, Hara in the intellect,
Brahmā in the ego-sense, the Lord of Devas (Śiva) in the two hands,
Agni and Yama in speech, and Prajāpati in the generative organ.
One should likewise place Vāyu in the skin, Sūrya in the eyes,
Varuṇa on the tongue, and the goddess Bhūmi in the nose.
A wise person should constantly maintain the mind upon Śiva— the bliss of awakening at the conclusion of all scriptures within the Puruṣa— for the purification of all sins.
Just as this dhāraṇā has been taught by those who know all the scriptures:
having withdrawn the effects, beginning with Brahmā, each into their own respective causes.
A person should directly hold the Praṇava within the complete Self— that which is the cause of all, unmanifest, indefinable, and insentient.
This is declared by the righteous who have mastered the Vedas to be the supreme concentration:
having withdrawn the senses, one should fix the mind upon the Self.
O one of great wisdom, for some time this *dhāraṇī* has been honored;
from the Veda alone the gods are sustained, from the Veda alone men always [sustain],
from the Veda alone the worlds always [sustain], and from the Veda alone Maheśvara [is sustained].
Having thus established the mind, that too is proclaimed as *dhāraṇā*:
"I am Brahman alone; I am neither a Gandharva, nor a god, nor a Yakṣa, nor a human."
It is neither the body, senses, intellect, and so forth, nor illusion, nor other deities; having established this through such understanding, it is proclaimed as *dhāraṇā*.
Thus everything has been fully explained, O you who are proficient in all the scriptures.
Thus ends the fifth chapter, titled "The Exposition of Withdrawal and Concentration," in the Yogasaṃgraha.
Meditation. In the *Yogasāramañjarī*:
"Now, therefore, I shall fully explain the unsurpassed yoga of meditation for those yogis who have not yet perfected their practice but desire its cultivation."
One should contemplate the body situated within the belly, resembling the stainless, brilliant, cool-rayed moon; by doing so for one month, wrinkles and graying hair are destroyed.
The Lord is seated within the lotus of the heart, possessing a radiance equal to the rising sun,
his body embraced by the Goddess who has a complexion like that of refined gold.
With all his limbs smeared with ashes and wearing a deer skin,
he is seated in the lotus posture, peaceful, three-eyed, and crowned by the moon.
Śiva, whose forehead is bathed in the divine nectar flowing from the crescent moon,
who holds the gestures of granting boons and fearlessness, the great axe, and the deer, and who bears the seal of the deer-mark.
The Supreme Lord is serene, holding a rosary and a book,
with his matted locks bound by the hoods of great serpents.
Endowed with youth and vigor, having swallowed the fear of death and other such things,
he has a beautiful face, lovely in all his limbs, and is the domain of protected, secret knowledge.
It shatters the flood of bonds that bind the individual soul, it is the savior from the ocean of worldly existence,
the bestower of the capacity for omniscience and other perfections, and the granter of all spiritual accomplishments.
Thus one should meditate upon Mahādeva for the pacification of all obstacles;
or else, one should meditate upon Śiva thus, within the doubly purified lotus of the heart.
Resembling pure crystal, possessing the radiance of ten thousand autumn moons,
holding a rosary, peaceful, gracious, bestowing boons, and auspicious.
It pacifies all death, destroys wrinkles and graying hair,
and rains down divine nectar from all sides like a great shower.
One should contemplate one's own body as suddenly freed from the burning pains of suffering by the falling rain of that nectar, which is cooling in nature.
By means of this yoga of meditation, one is liberated from the bondage of the body;
[one perceives] within the center of the pericarp of the heart-lotus a nectar in the form of a lamp-flame.
The yogi should contemplate the entire triple world being pervaded by a great light that has arisen, surpassing the rays of the moon.
By this yoga of meditation, the yogi shall himself become a lord.
The yogi should contemplate his own body as possessing a radiance equal to ten million suns;
through the complete non-differentiation from the Self, he shall soon attain yoga.
The yogi should contemplate himself as the perfect form of the Lord;
by the power of that meditation, he shall attain the pure accomplishment of the illustrious Śāmbhavī.
"I am Śiva; I am immeasurable; I am inconceivable; I am the Great.
In this manner, during the practice of meditation, one should meditate upon the Self, which possesses all forms.
In the *Praṇavacintāmaṇi*:

"I am the glorious ocean of nectar, whose quarters are filled by the rising of the moon of bliss; its divine waters are colored by the foam of the essence of consciousness; and it is inhabited by the various classes of Pramathas and deities as its fish."
One whose self is shaken free from defilement.
In this body-temple, where the mountains of fear born of sin have been shattered by the diamond-like pollen of the lotus feet of the glorious Guru,
I remember the supreme, great form of the Self, which resembles ten million moons and suns yet is as subtle as an atom.
Resplendent as a thousand flashes of lightning, resembling a mote of dust in its subtlety,
intensely gladdened by the density of bliss, accessible through meditative experience,
and the immeasurable means for attaining the ocean of nectar.
May I not forget this excellent awakening within my heart.
Like a flash of lightning, that light which rises upward by splitting open the door-panels of the crowns of the six lotuses,
rains down a thousand showers of thick, nectar-like fluid.
O Megha, I worship the lamp of the Supreme Self within my heart.
His body is sprinkled by the gathering of droplets from his own bliss, a mass of waves nourished by the very nature of consciousness;
his mental activity is stainless, supreme, and accessible through true being.
I am an ocean of the nectar of arts, ever eager for service.
Since this entire universe, consisting of earth, sky, air, fire, and the divisions of the sun, has its expansive reality as one,
that which is the cause of all, infinite, inconceivable, and primordial— [...is that Brahman.]
In this [state], consciousness is luminous and transcends mind and speech.
That which has the Veda as its root, all the scriptures as its leaves and stalks,
bliss as its tawny hue, and the nectar of immortality as its divine essence;
I am the bee upon the lotus-heart of that yogi, which shines with the eightfold manifestation of the Siddhas.
By this practice of meditation, one may attain liberation while living;
through meditation one obtains yoga, and from meditation comes even that perfection which is difficult to achieve.
By means of meditation, moreover, one may cross over death—my word is not false. Thus it is said.
In the Sūtasamhitā:
"Now, therefore, I shall fully explain the unsurpassed yoga of meditation:
[one should contemplate] that which is stainless, white, radiant, and very cool in the sky."
Having meditated upon the full moon-maṇḍala as an immovable object within the field of vision,
one should contemplate Mahādeva in its center, whose form is supreme bliss.
Bestowing boons with half of his body joined to Umā, devoid of birth and sustenance,
resembling pure crystal, adorned with a crescent moon,
three-eyed, four-armed, blue-necked, and higher than the highest.
O best among the knowers of Brahman, one should constantly meditate: "I am eternally His servant."
Alternatively, [one should meditate] upon the full solar disc, shining and most beautiful, situated in the midst of space and extending for a hundred thousand yojanas.
The Lord, the creator of all the worlds, who has the form of gold,
with golden beard and hair, and likewise golden nails.
With a face like a hibiscus flower, blue-necked and deep red,
he is renowned even among cowherds as one whose body is half that of Ambikā.
A person should constantly meditate on "I am He" during the periods of twilight, or else [meditate]:
"I am Hari himself, the omniscient Supreme Person."
The Puruṣa has a thousand heads, a thousand eyes, and a thousand feet;
he is the universal Lord Nārāyaṇa, the imperishable, the supreme state.
Or rather, O observer of noble vows, he is Brahman—the infinite, whose nature is existence, consciousness, and bliss.
One should cultivate the intention "I am He" for the sake of liberation;
whoever should meditate even for a moment upon this Lord of Gods within the heart.
"Because Brahman is of the nature of the witness, this [world] is not [Brahman]," so says the Śruti. Thus, in the Sāragītā:
"In the center of the lotus of the heart is the lamp, the essence of non-duality..."

"He who meditates even once with his mind upon me— who am composed of the *praṇava*, inconceivable, sought through yoga by yogins, the union of Hari, Guru, and Śiva, and the one who dwells within all beings— he is liberated. Thus it is said.
In the *Yogasāramañjarī*:
One should meditate upon the pure lunar disc in the center of the heart, dripping nectar;
with that nectar, one should [bathe] one's own body from the soles of the feet to the crown of the head.
One should visualize one's own body being flooded and satisfy it with that nectar.
O Goddess worshipped by the gods, within three seasons there shall be firmness, delicacy, the destruction of disease, and the removal of wrinkles and grey hair.
In the region below the lotus-seat and above the opening of the *kha-ra*,
one should visualize the previously mentioned Maṇḍaleśī, accompanied by a shower of nectar.
From the root-seed, through the emergence of showers of cool nectar from the petals,
one should not perceive anything as being outside or inside that which is merged within the ocean of nectar.
But the entire internal [impurity] is [cleansed] by the supreme nectars emerging from the moon at the aperture of Brahmā (brahmarandhra), which enter and pervade the channels within that aperture.
One should satisfy one's own life-force (jīva) and the deities with the thought that they are Śiva; having contemplated that the entire internal organ is filled by the rain of that nectar,
it issues forth through ten million channels known as the paths of the hair-pores (svaromākhya).
One should contemplate [the deity] as being anointed both externally and internally with showers of nectar.
Therein, O Śivā, one should satisfy with the nectar of one's own self the entire universe, which has emerged from the center as identical with that [self] and consists of that very essence.
One should contemplate this entire universe as one's own body, completely satisfied by that nectar, and consisting of the intellect of supreme bliss.
One should wrap it with one's own vein, which is unctuous and cool, using lime plaster.
By this yoga, O Goddess, after six months, one becomes free from old age and death;
[one attains] the ninth color, red, which possesses the bindu and is of the nature of nectar.
Having meditated upon the eyes, one should contemplate the entire universe as being offered into one's own body by means of the rays of those showers of nectar.
Through the practice of meditation for three years with a non-conceptual mind,
the world at the end of seven times seven [forty-nine kalpas] and seven births are seen.
The letter *ro* is the syllable *ha*; the ninth letter is *sa*. Thus: *hrīṃ sūryamaṇḍalāya namaḥ* for the right eye, and *sa somamaṇḍalāya namaḥ* for the left eye.
[One should contemplate: "In the ocean of milk, my own body is blue."
For one who contemplates this constantly for a year, there is the destruction of the lines of wrinkles;
by means of the streams of supreme nectar flowing from the stream of immortality at the aperture of Brahma (brahmarandhra).
Within six months, one whose body has been transfigured effects the destruction of wrinkles and grey hair;
his own body becomes like the moon, free from blemish and composed of nectar.
By meditating for half a year, the yogi becomes free from wrinkles and gray hair;
he becomes like the orb of the sun when heated, yet not touched by the spots or the nectar of the moon.
One should contemplate [the deities] within the seven lotuses from the base (mūla) to the aperture of Brahmā (brahmarandhra), according to the sequence of numbers four,
six, ten, twelve, sixteen, two, and so forth.
One should meditate on [the deity] as being flooded with nectar by means of the leaves inscribed with syllables;
one should contemplate the unity of these mandalas in their proper sequence.
O Pārvatī, from an uninterrupted stream extending as far as the cosmic egg (brahmāṇḍa),
one perceives one's own body as consisting of that [light], shining with the brilliance of ten million moons.
The yogi should contemplate [the object] as sprinkled with nectar for the sake of attaining success in yoga.

O beloved, one obtains the destruction of wrinkles and graying hair within six months; one whose desires for gain have been destroyed is freed from the poison of suffering by the *dhātrī* fruit; omniscience is attained in one year, and in three years, one becomes like the Lord.
"O divine one, the state of moving through the sky (khecaratva) shall come to be, honored by the [eight siddhis] beginning with Maṇimat," thus it is said in the Śivagaurī-saṃvāda.
O Dear One, the solar mandala is situated between the two lovers.
If a person meditates for the duration of one month, the mass of his diseases shall be destroyed.
Within six months, one attains equality with Indra; after a year, one becomes equal to Viṣṇu.
From six years, there will be equality with the speed of sound; from twelve years, one becomes exceedingly radiant—if one meditates with a restrained mind, this contemplation will indeed bear fruit.
O Goddess, by meditating for only half a year upon that which resides in the center of the red egg, overflowing with red nectar, one indeed becomes free from old age and death.
O Goddess, one should meditate on the Mūlādhāra as a blazing solar orb;
one should contemplate the body as being pervaded by the mass of its radiance.

In the same manner, one should constantly meditate upon one's own body as being joined together by their mutual radiance— the primary image in the *brahmarandhra*, the image in the heart-lotus, and the image in the heart that has likewise reached the *brahmarandhra*. Each of these is situated separately within the heart-lotus and the *brahmarandhra* respectively.
Day after day, one should contemplate the body as being composed of that [element] up to the limits of space.
Within six months, one shall attain mastery over the powers such as atomization (aṇimā) and others;
and within three years, resembling the sun, one attains omniscience.
One should meditate on the individual soul (jīva) within that reflection, having the form of a blazing lamp-flame;
within a month, it removes wrinkles and grey hair, as well as death, disease, and fear.
Having attained omniscience after a year, one should dwell in the upper courtyard of the sky;
there, one should contemplate one's own life-force (jīva) as established in the state of the light-linga (jyotir-liṅga).
By that, one should contemplate the entire egg as filled with nectar;
therein, the yogi situated in the center is filled with the quality known as fragrance.
One should not forget the principle of earth (dharātattva), which is the support of all things without exception;
nor the principle of water (jalatattva) in its entirety, which is the support of the qualities of the essence of speech.
O Goddess of the gods, the best of those who know yoga should contemplate that entire principle of radiant energy (tejas-tattva), which is the substratum of such qualities, within his three eyes.
O Śivā, one should contemplate the entire element of air within a mere breath,
and the entirety of the element of space, which is endowed with the quality known as sound.
O Goddess, at the place of hearing (the ears), one should remember [the process], having withdrawn the external [senses] by means of the flavors;
one should remember the body, consisting of the universe, merged within the interior of the egg of flames.
This imperishable universe, from its smallest atom to its final dissolution, is merged within the center of one's own body; may he swallow it through the play of Time.
Having bound the elements, such as water and earth, very firmly through their unification, one should meditate upon the lotus posture (*padmāsana*).
One should contemplate liberation from the impurities of time and the body free from disease.
O Īśānī, when one meditates upon that Egg as being devoid of any cavity,
then, having abandoned the fear of time, one may dwell according to one's own will like Śiva.
By this yoga, O Goddess, one may deceive the approaching time of death;
having taken possession of the principles beginning with earth, one remains free from affliction.
O Pārvatī, hear now the fruit of this meditation through its equal application:
one may shatter mountains, trees, and the like, and dry up the lords of the waters.
The yogi brings about the quelling of the flames of the terrible fire of time;
he conquers the principle of sound (śabdatattva), which is free from old age and death.
"One who knows the three times becomes himself the agent and attains omnipresence. Thus says Gorakṣa.
He who constantly keeps his eyes half-closed and likewise half-open,
and perceives Brahman with the eye of the mind— he is the sovereign of yogis.
Situated between the moon and the sun, and between the two stars by its brilliance,
one should practice the Brahma-star by joining the two points (bindus).
Intent upon the vision of Brahman within the external, internal, and intermediate objects of focus,
behold indeed those forms, both seen and unseen.
From the root-tuber attached to the stalk, the Brahma-nāḍī emerges with the luster of the moon;
in its center is [the energy] resembling ten million flashes of lightning, which ascends upwards.
One should mentally perceive the form as being similar to a lotus fiber;
one should remember it as extending up to the aperture of Brahmā (brahmarandhra) and bestowing spiritual perfection.
Likewise, the yogi should always mentally perceive the object of focus above the forehead within the Kollāṭa-maṇḍala as having the form of a shimmering star;
or else, he should block the two openings of the ears with his two index fingers.
And within his glorious body, he hears the resonance of the *nāda*, sounding like the cry of a *ghūghū* bird.
Likewise, one should perceive the form of intense blue in the middle of the eye;
this is to be known as the internal object of focus (antarlakṣya). Now hear about the external object of focus (bahirlakṣya).
From the tip of the nose, at distances of four, six, ten, and twelve finger-breadths respectively,
one should visualize externally the five subtle elements (tanmātras) as blue, smoky-grey, red, wave-like (white), and yellow.
Or how might one perceive the space directly before them with a steady gaze?
Rays of light are seen by yogis of tranquil mind.
Whether at the tip of the nose or in the corner of the eye, when the yogi’s gaze perceives the ground as resembling molten gold, his vision becomes steady.
Alternatively, at a distance of twelve finger-breadths above the navel, one should perceive a form resembling a mass of light; this shall be the bestower of liberation.
Or wherever the yogi may be, there he should observe that very space;
his mind becomes just like that.
Thus has been described the manifold external object of focus;
now hear the description of the intermediate object of focus as previously taught by the wise.

Then, one should observe white and other colors, as well as disks resembling fierce moonlight, lightning, or the crest of a flame; or one may perceive a single blazing void devoid of ground—that indeed is the central object of focus.
One should perceive [the Self] as formless and devoid of qualities, like the sky; or as the form of the body, intensely radiant with a vast and supreme space;
or as Mahākāla, resembling the dark wind and exceedingly brilliant.
It has the form of ultimate reality, resembling the sun and moon, and is situated in the center of space.
"This is indeed the fivefold void; its state exists both externally and internally.
The man who perceives this within the focal point becomes like that very void.
Thus it is said in the *Yogasāramañjarī*.

Thus, for one who has withdrawn all objects of the mind and remains for a long time in the Great Yoga— the sole cause of the nectar of the state of pure consciousness— which is the self of the entire universe without exception;

Alas, yogis desire to emerge from this universe— which is like a single drop in the ocean of my own golden body, like a firefly before the sun, and like the egg of an ant— just as one might wish to escape from such a place!
In the Vāsiṣṭha:
"The contemplation that 'I am indeed pure consciousness alone' is called meditation (dhyāna);
the non-forgetting of that meditation is correctly designated as samādhi."
Thus ends the sixth chapter, titled "The Nature of the Object of Meditation," in the Yogasārasaṃgraha.
In the *Uttaragītā*:
"Devoid of valid cognition, devoid of mind, devoid of intellect, free from affliction,
entirely empty, and formless— this is the characteristic of his samādhi."
Having placed the mind in space and having made the mind supportless,
one should know that partless state to be the characteristic of one established in samādhi.
In the *Dṛgdṛśyaviveka*:
"Having set aside name and form, one whose characteristic is Being-Consciousness-Bliss (saccidānanda) should always practice samādhi, whether within the heart or externally."
In the heart, samādhi is of two kinds: with conceptualization (savikalpa) and without conceptualization (nirvikalpa).
Furthermore, that with conceptualization is twofold, being permeated by either the visible object or by sound.
One should meditate on the conscious Self as the witness of desire and the rest, which are born of the mind and are objects of perception;
this is savikalpaka samādhi, permeated by the perceived object.
"Free from attachment, being consciousness-bliss, self-luminous, and devoid of duality— this state, pierced by the word 'it exists,' is *savikalpaka* samādhi."
Due to immersion in the essence of one's own direct experience, one disregards both visible objects and sounds;
thus, non-conceptual samādhi arises, like a lamp placed in a windless spot.
Whether by day or by night, in an external location, and with regard to any object whatsoever,
when there is the first meditative concentration (*samādhi*), name-and-form (*nāmarūpa*) becomes distinct from that [object] alone.
"This reality is an undivided single essence, being existence-consciousness-bliss and immutable"— this uninterrupted contemplation constitutes middling samādhi.
The flavors of the state of becoming a pillar (stambhībhāva-rasa) have been described; the third [stage] is considered as before.
One should spend time continuously with these six meditative absorptions (samādhis).
In the Śivayoga:
when the vital breath is completely exhausted and the mind is dissolved.
When there is a state of equal flavor, that is designated as samādhi.
Patañjali:
And that state of the mind which is devoid of fluctuations and abides in the form of Brahman is designated as the samādhi known as "asamprajñāta" (superconscious).
In Haṭhayoga:
"That state in which there is equality— the oneness of the individual self (jīvātman) and the supreme self (paramātman)—
and in which all volitional thoughts have perished, is designated as samādhi."
In the Bhagavadgītā: "As a lamp in a windless place does not flicker— this is the simile remembered for the yogi of restrained mind who practices the yoga of the Self."
In the Vāsiṣṭha:
"The realization of reality alone is said to be the fire that burns all desires like straw;
it is designated by the word 'samādhi,' but not merely remaining silent."
One perceives this collection of qualities as being without self;
that inner coolness which arises is called samādhi.
But he who delights in the Self alone, performing the functions of all the senses in solitude, and who is neither affected by joy nor sorrow— he is said to be composed.
Such a one is ever-composed, eternally satisfied, and perceives the reality of things as they truly are.
That which is called "supreme wisdom" (parā-prajñā) by the wise through the term "samādhi"—

unshakable, free from egoism, and not subject to the protection [of duality] amidst pairs of opposites— that is the supreme state, established in the non-establishment of even that which is established, denoted by the word "samādhi."
That which is free from certainty, preference, desire, and the distinction between what is to be abandoned and what is to be adopted is called "perfectly complete" by the term *samādhi*.
In the Sūtasamhitā:
"Now, therefore, I shall fully explain Samādhi, which destroys the [mental] count [of fluctuations].
Samādhi is the arising of consciousness toward the supreme unity of the individual soul."
I am neither the body, nor the vital breaths, nor likewise the sense organs.
I am not the mind, nor the intellect, nor indeed the heart, nor the ego;
I am not the ego-sense, nor the earth, nor water, nor fire, nor likewise air.
Neither is it space, nor sound, nor touch, nor taste;
neither is it smell, nor form, nor am I illusion, nor am I memory.
"O best of sages, that state of mind which realizes, 'I am indeed Śiva alone, because my true nature is eternally manifest,' is here called samādhi."
"I am neither Brahmā nor a transmigrating being; there is never anything other than me"—one should know one's own Self thus; that is proclaimed as Samādhi.
Alternatively, O best of yogis, one should know the Lord whose self is the Praṇava as consisting of the three phonemes, namely the triad beginning with the letter ‘A’.
It is said in the *Praṇavacintāmaṇi*:
"The letter *ha* is declared to be Śambhu, and the letter *sa* is said to be Śakti. The Moon, who exists in the form of Śakti, flows through the left channel (*vāmanāḍī*)."
The Sun, in the form of Śambhu, flows through the right channel (nāḍī).
The essence of Brahman is the middle between the two; it is the savior, O Bala.
In the *Tāpanīya*: "The letter 'a' is the Puruṣa therein, and the letter 'm' is said to be Prakṛti;
likewise, the Praṇava, the syllable Oṃ, is remembered as the Puruṣa whose essence is the seed."
"The letter *ma* is the nature (*prakṛti*) because it has the form of power (*śakti*), and it possesses the form of the noble one (*ārya*).
Since it exists in the form of the nature of male and female, it always resides in the midst of form.
Thus, the single-syllable *tāra* clearly arises from the two syllables.
From that, the five-syllabled [mantra] arose, containing a collection of fifty letters.
In the *Kalāsaṃhitā*:

"The first vowel, the fifth [vowel], the end of the *pavarga* class, followed by that, and then the *bindu* and *nāda*—this five-syllabled [mantra] is declared to be known as the *praṇava*. Thus it is said.
In the Śāradātilaka:
"The sixteen digits born of Nāda are remembered as arising from the vowel 'a';
ten are produced from the vowel 'u', and another ten from the vowel 'm'."
From those two as well, others are born in the sequence of parts and colors;
first, the *praṇava* manifests in the form of subtle creation, and by means of that form, it is expanded (*brahmate*).
In the *Praṇavacintāmaṇi*:
"The sixteen measures (mātrās) are likewise afflicted by the downward breaths;
the best of yogis should practice all that which has been perfected as Brahman."
Both possess the state of being seven mātrās less than sixteen, that is, eight mātrās.
Because it is established as belonging to the Moon alone, the supreme state consists of sixteen mātrās:
the letter *a*, then *u*, and after that, *m*.
From that [the half-measure], then the resonance (nāda), then the point (bindu), then the digits (kalā);
then power (śakti), peace (śānti), equanimity (samatā), the state beyond mind (unmanā), and the one who transcends mind (manonmanī).
Vaikharī, Madhyamā, Paśyantī, and then Parā;
these are declared to be the sixteen Mātrās, and the Tāraka is endowed with them.
The pure *praṇava* is proclaimed to consist of sixteen *mātrās*. The letter *A*, however, is said to consist of twenty-four principles (*tattvas*).
The letter *u* is clearly composed of twenty-six principles (*tattvas*);
the letter *ma* is proclaimed to be endowed with thirty-eight principles;
and the half-measure (*ardhamātrā*) is declared in the scriptures to consist of eighty-six principles.
Nāda consists of seventy principles; Bindu consists of thirty-two;
Śakti is said to consist of twenty-six principles, including the eighteen principles of Kalā.
The peaceful state (*śānti*), consisting of thirty principles, is the most excellent and brings victory;
thereafter, it is said that the equal state (*samānā*) consists of twenty-five principles.
Unmanā, who abides in the world, is the speaker of the sixty-four principles;
Manonmanī has as her sphere of experience the twenty-four renowned principles;
and Vaikharī, which deludes the universe, is the expansion of the fifty principles.
The Madhyamā, whose nature consists of twenty-eight principles, is the state of all abodes;
the Paśyantī is said to have the form of four, eight, and one principles.
She, who abides in the supreme reality of bliss, is declared to be the Upaniṣad according to the sequence [of the scriptures];
she is known even by those who have mastered the entire sequence of all the Upaniṣads.
Thus, by means of these sixteen enumerations, there is the determination of that reality and so forth.
The syllable Oṃ consisting of seventeen mātrās is the savior, the source of the stars;
the syllable Oṃ consisting of sixteen mātrās is Śambhu, the savior, the eternal.
Varṇava, Praṇava, Tāra, Tāraka, Yogapa, Dhruva, and the third Oṃkāra— these are proclaimed as the various forms of the Praṇava.
He alone who knows that which has transcended the sixteen coverings— the guiding star, fixed and imperishable,
consisting of the phonemes, the principles, and the scriptures— is indeed I.
Oṃkāra, Praṇava, Tāra, the third, Tāraka, Dhruva,
Rudra, Īśāna, Akṣara, the all-pervading Anta, and then Vaidyuta.
Śukla, Sūkṣma, Para-Brahman, and Bhagavān— these are the eight incarnations proclaimed by Śaṅkarī according to the sequence of the Praṇava Upaniṣad.
In the Śaiva Tantra, regarding the division of the sixteen kalās: "The letter *a*, the letter *u*, and the letter *m* immediately following that..."
The Praṇava consists of the half-mora, as well as Nāda, Bindu, and Kalā; then Śakti, Śānti, Samanā, Unmanā, and from that, Vaikharī, Madhyamā, Paśyantī, and Parā— these are its natural states.
"Yogins know that the sixteenth [digit] is joined with sixteen mātrās. Thus it is said. In the *Praṇavacintāmaṇi*:
"One should know that the syllable 'A' is the word *tvaṃ*; they know the syllable 'U' to be the word *tat*."
The letter *m* is the eighty-first; thus this becomes the *praṇava*.
The word "thou" (*tvaṃ*) is the great statement (*mahāvākya*), and the *praṇava* is that word, O beloved.
Because of the oneness of the half-measure and so forth, the supreme Praṇava is proclaimed;
likewise, in that state, there was no distinction between the individual self (jīvātman) and the supreme self (paramātman).
Having attained oneness through the *praṇava*, the ascetic shall reach his true nature.
The *bindu* is said to be the word "thou" (*tvaṃ-pada*), while the half-measure (*ardhamātrā*) is indeed the word "that" (*tat-pada*).
The sound [of the letter] *a* arises from the throat; from that, one should become the supreme *nāda*. From the navel-cavity, the letter *u* flashes forth with a short measure;
from the middle position, the letter *m* enters through the sense organs and arises from the throat.
The Nāda arises from the center, Śakti from the head, and the Pada from the end; the Śānti extends to the dvādaśānta.
He whose form is the meditation on the Oṃkāra, the leader of the world, the lord of the sun and the sky, is the embodiment of the universe.
In the *Narasiṃhatāpanīya*:
"The entire Veda and so forth have as their root that which resides in the thirteenth of the vowels, having the form of the moon and the bindu.
I bow to the Praṇava, which is endowed with the Vedas, has the form of a slumbering serpent, and is the root of the Three Jewels.
In the *Yogasāramañjarī*: "In the *mūlādhāra*, one should remember the syllable *Tāra* (Om), possessing the luster of an unswerving flash of lightning—
the Goddess Śakti, the primordial *Manonmanī*, who is the radiance of consciousness and the source of all."
The sequence of phonemes, possessing the splendor of ten million rising suns and having the nature of the consciousness of the mantra,
has emerged from the blazing consciousness of individual manifestation.
One should remember the Goddess as blazing, having the form of a star, and full of splendor—
the Goddess from whom the sprout of that life-force has emerged, appearing like a spark of fire.
And then, O Dear One, one should utter the mantra in the form of sound within the heart.
Of the mantra endowed with the consciousness of the individual soul (jīva) and having the form of light,
there arises from the head of Brahmā the power of the individual soul (jīva-śakti), beginning with the syllable *dhruva*.
O Goddess, through the aforementioned accumulation, one should extract the consciousness of the living soul—
the God whose nature is the primordial principle (āditattva) and who illumines the consciousness of Śakti.
The king of mantras, possessed of great splendor, which consists of the entirety of the garland of phonemes.
With hair flowing in a single direction, broad-chested, and greatly patient;
with a turban whose crest-point is turned upward, and its topknot formed by that very bindu.
Endowed with infinite power, possessing great radiance and great forbearance,
he instantly devours the entirety of Śiva’s power.
"One should then remember [the light] as very steady within one's own body, blazing even more intensely,
merged in the center of one's own body, until the release of the breath. Thus,
by the splendor of the Supreme Lord, from the mouth of Kuṇḍalinī, as it is beyond the supreme...

Just as bubbles arise from the mouth of a frog in the water, so too do the fifty phonemes emerge. Having uttered them in the form of *vaikharī* beginning with the *praṇava*, they exist in the *mūlādhāra* as the nature of Śiva and Śakti; for they know the form of Kuṇḍalinī to be like a fire that produces bliss.
Due to the conjunction with the vital breath and fire that has arisen, it is therefore designated as "nāda" (sound).
In the *Praṇavacintāmaṇi*:
"Nāda is said to be twofold, namely the struck (*āhata*) and the unstruck (*anāhata*).
The unstruck nāda is devoid of qualities (*nirguṇa*), while the struck is traditionally held to possess qualities (*saguṇa*)."
The sound that is devoid of attributes shines forth from the King within the lotus-heart of every living being;
when intensely impelled, it is the sole means for attaining liberation alone.
The first is the sound of Brahman, supreme and heart-delighting, an ocean of supreme bliss;
the second is the qualified sound, consisting of vocal, whispered, and mental recitation.
Being the primary cause for all goals and the sole delighter of the entire world,
it is expounded in the treatises on singing, instrumental music, and the art of dramatic performance.
Impelled everywhere by its manifold forms, it shines forth;
indeed, as mere sound, it exists everywhere—whether vocal, whispered, or mental.
The resonance of Brahman (brahmanāda) is said to be mental and vocal singing;
it consists of the expanded, the stretched, the enveloped, the opened, the raised, and the kumbhaka.
The *plutānanda*, *plutānanda*, and *navanāda* are proclaimed;
they were demonstrated by Prahlāda for the purpose of facing toward Nṛsiṃha,
[accompanied] by the acute (*udātta*), the grave (*anudātta*), the circumflex (*svarita*), and the *pracaya* accent.
"By singing [this], practitioners obtain each respective fruit," so says Nārada. [The fruits are:
the melting of stone, the sharpening of intelligence, the bringing of rain, the manifestation of deities within a stone, and the flowing of milk from cows.
It causes flowers to bloom in trees even out of season,
and it utterly deludes all people, as well as beasts, deer, and birds.
"These arise for practitioners from that meditation in an instant.
Having understood this, the peaceful practitioner, following the instructions of the Guru,
should practice with a tranquil mind in a secluded place for the sake of attaining the perfection of Nāda.

Yogis declare that the sound of Brahman— which destroys birth and old age, is as enchanting as a flute once filled with wind, and resounds incessantly within the hearts of all embodied beings— arises from the apertures.
Thus it is said in the Dhyānanādabindūpaniṣad: "That which is the unstruck sound (anāhata), and that which is beyond that sound— when the yogi perceives that supreme reality, his doubts are severed."
Having conquered the six internal enemies— difficult to overcome and incurable—
by means of the attainment of knowledge and dispassion, and being endowed with faith;
Having entered a secluded and inaccessible place, graced by supreme bliss,
he assumed the svāstika posture, preceded by the purification of the earth.
Having performed obeisance to the guru and others, one should be devoted to *prāṇāyāma* through the correct practice of exhalation (*recaka*),
inhalation (*pūraka*), and retention (*kumbhaka*) with short, long, and protracted durations.
Having emitted [the breath] three times once, and then again three times repeatedly;
having uttered it three times once, preceded by six breath-restraints (prāṇāyāma).
Concentrated in meditation, one who knows the reality and understands the truth should contemplate his own body as having the form of the syllable Om, and then visualize it as consisting of light.
Having performed three breath-controls (prāṇāyāmas), one should contemplate [the Self] separately within oneself.
Śrī Kṛṣṇa said:
"Having drawn up the heart-lotus which is facing downward by means of the *praṇava*, it reaches the interior of the lotus-calyx; then the *vyāhṛtis* cause it to blossom once again."
Within that is fire; within the fire is the sun;
within the sun is the moon; and within the moon is the radiance.
In the *Dhyānanādabindūpaniṣad*:
"Therein, one should contemplate fire, sun, and moon, each situated one above the other.
The bindu is situated in the midst of the radiance; the nāda is the sound situated within that.
"In the *Dhyānanāda*: 'The supreme [state] beyond the seed-syllable is the Bindu; the supreme of that is known as the Nāda.
Thus it is said in the *Praṇavacintāmaṇi*.
During the repetitions of the Praṇava, by means of the wind that is restrained and then raised up, [the breath is controlled].
Because there is no movement elsewhere, even when struck it is not struck;
the drop is pierced by the resonance (nāda), and that resonance is pierced by bliss (sukha).
In the *Uttaragītā*:
"Of that unstruck sound (*anāhata-śabda*) there is the resonance (*dhvani*);
within the resonance is the light (*jyotis*), and within the light is the mind (*manas*)."
That mind dissolves through the resonance of the sound of the syllable Om, up until the withdrawal of the vital breath; that is the supreme state of Viṣṇu.
"Having raised [the mind] without support, one has gone there to the state of resonance (nāda).
Thus: "One should meditate on the mindless (amanaska) at the navel, the heart, the head, or the center;
in that center is Brahman—so the noble ones, the best among those who know yoga, maintain."
O crusher of asuras, know that the Supreme Brahman is the subtle sound (nāda), which exists in manifold ways and many forms, and whose nature is latent within all things.
Know that the letter *u* is contained within the letter *a*, and the letter *m* is situated in its center;
it is said to be dissolved (*līna*) and endowed with the three forms (*mūrti*).
In the midst of that is what is called the *bindu*, and from the center of that arises the resonance (*dhvani*).
The radiance is contained within sound; the sun is contained within that radiance;
Sthāṇu is situated in the center of the sun; and the mind is situated in the center of Sthāṇu.
That mind dissolves, and that resonance is called Brahman;
this entire world of moving and non-moving beings is enveloped by that sound.
In the *Praṇavacintāmaṇi*: "O Dear One,
[this occurs] day and night even among all stationary things, among moving beings,
and even within the multitude of creatures from ants up to Brahmā."
"Enveloping both within and without, the Nāda remains alone.
Thus, it is unattainable for practitioners, like a fruit in the palm of one's hand.
Free from doubt, there are thirty-two states of perfect bliss through various specific distinctions, each by itself.
Whether taken individually or collectively, and whether in their natural or established states, they produce accomplishment.
One should practice the *praṇava* with the "leaping" (*pluta*) and "non-leaping" (*apluta*) [utterances], and likewise with its front portion consisting of half a measure (*mātrā*).
Just as by means of the "leaping over the stage" (*raṅgapluta*), one attains perfection through that very limb—the resonance (*nāda*) situated at the front—by means of its half-measure.
Having made the *praṇava*— consisting of the half-mora (*ardhamātra*) pervaded by *nāda*— face [the practitioner] at the end of the night,

it should be meditated upon daily by the best of adepts as arising from the lotus of their own heart, shining within the space of the sky of their own heart, having been brought forth from its own support through the method of practicing the incomparable wind (*pavana*) in the eight lotuses.
"Mitra, Vinihata, Dhṛtikṛt, Sāvadhāna, and Paritrāt"—thus [it is said]. (p.
48) [These names] also apply individually to the sixteen locations ending with Ājñā.
From the letter 'a' to the letter 'kṣa', they imitate both the manifest and the unmanifest.
Having correctly understood the musical notes (*svaras*), a person should daily restrain the breath according to the intervals prescribed therein—
by means of low (*mandra*), middle (*madhyama*), and high (*tāra*) pitches,
as well as by acute (*udātta*), grave (*anudātta*), circumflex (*svarita*), and protracted (*pracaya*) accents.
In the heart, through the conjunction with lamps ablaze and according to the respective sequences taught, the practitioner attains mastery;
each individual vowel, from beginning to end, is reduced to the remainder of the sixteen stages.
Having performed the five types of *pluta-udātta* and the clearly articulated *mapluta*, and having attained the nectar of sound (*nādāmṛta*), one forgets the entire world as if in a dream.
O Lord of the ten vowels, by contemplating each [syllable] from beginning to end with undivided intellect, multiplied fourfold, one attains unfeigned liberation that removes rebirth.
The yogi, through the practice of nāda-samādhi, should thus revolve [the breath] starting from the previously mentioned short [vowel] and ending with the supreme (parā).
Having abandoned exhalation and inhalation, with his vision fixed upon the lotus feet of the Guru in a state of perfect yoga, he— like a bee humming within the interval of pure *kumbhaka*—
leaped and was submerged; forgetting everything, the knower of the Self remained motionless like the sky, free from the sense of "mine."

"The one who delights in the play of the *galaharī* [throat-ornament] is the sound (*nāda*) within the nectar of the bliss of one's own heart. Thus it is said. In the *Nādasaṃgraha*: "Having understood the fivefold *śuddhapluta*, one should divide the fivefold *raṅgapluta*."
Having quadrupled [the vowels], one should practice the ten protracted vowels (*pluta*) as taught for the ten sounds.

"One should practice after knowing the designations of the consonants, such as the half-mora (*ardhamātrā*), by means of the open *praṇava* [Oṃ], according to the sequence of the *raṅgapluta*, and not the long [vowel]. And in the *Vedalakṣaṇa*:
A short vowel should be understood as having one measure (mātra); a long vowel is said to have two measures;
a protracted vowel is known to have three measures; whereas a consonant has half a measure.

A consonant is said to have half the duration of a short vowel; its nasalized counterpart (anunāsika) has half of that. That very [nasalized sound] is rooted in the resonance (nāda) and is sung of as having the measure of half a mora (ardhamātrā). Thus says Śiva. A protracted (pluta) *tāra* consists of four moras and is comprised of three protracted units.
