With a complexion like a cloud in the sky, holding in her terrifying lotus-hands a trident, a khaṭvāṅga staff, a bell, a vajra, and an excellent skull-cup,
she [destroys] the entire host of evil spirits, ghosts, and kūśmāṇḍas.
For one who meditates upon the Lord, who is ever intent on grasping [all things], there shall be no fear.
Having meditated thus upon the Supreme Lord, one should recite the mantra eight thousand times;
thereby, one is liberated from all calamities, obstacles, and the like, along with diseases.
The mantra is the three-syllabled *Mṛtyuñjaya*.
Whoever recites this mantra with devotion twelve hundred thousand times shall be freed from wrinkles and grey hair, and indeed attain freedom from old age and death.
Having practiced the previously mentioned posture and sitting composed with senses subdued,
one should meditate upon the supreme reality with an unwavering inner self.
For the sake of removing all obstacles, one should first meditate upon the Great Body (Mahāvapuḥ),
whose feet are at the bottom of the netherworld (pātāla), whose body is the sky with its frown-brow,
whose head is the worlds beginning with heaven, and whose arms are the directions, consisting of the essence of the deities.
He whose eyes are the sun and the moon, who is adorned with the garlands of sacred fields,
whose garment is the ocean, and who pervades the wondrous abode of the universe.

One should meditate on this entire world of moving and non-moving beings, from Brahmā down to a blade of grass, as being within one's own pores; and one should meditate upon one's own body as consisting of the universe.
O Goddess, one should thus meditate upon the Great Form for the sake of attaining stability of mind.
Thus, as the yogin meditates correctly,
his mental fluctuations gradually attain stillness through the contemplation of divine knowledge.
Having thus stabilized the mind, one should commence that meditation;
one should meditate upon the supreme lotus in one's own heart, which consists of the nature of Śiva and Śakti.
The *tāraka* is the stalk of the *śakti*, the *prāsāda* is the pericarp,
the *agnimaṇḍala* is rich with petals, and the *sūryamaṇḍala* is the filaments.
The knower of the Self should long contemplate the lunar mandala, whose filaments are the supreme grace and whose pericarp is the union of Śiva and Śakti.
In the midst of that, for the sake of purifying the self, one should meditate upon the Supreme Lord,
who resembles a dark blue cloud and has great serpents bound in his matted locks.
The Lord, who has the crescent moon as his crest-ornament, who is formidable, whose face is pervaded by the sound "Hūṃ," who holds a sword,
a trident, the gesture of fearlessness, and a snake-noose.
He bears the skull-bowl, the bell, and the sword, and likewise bestows boons.
Wearing red garments, adorned with red garlands, and embellished with fragrances.
Wearing the great ornaments of eight serpents, roaring and destroying fear,
he is clothed in a tiger skin with a lion skin as his upper garment.
Adorned with ornaments such as anklets, necklaces, and other finery,
his three eyes were the moon, the sun, and fire, and his fangs emitted flames.
It devours all the millions of faults and obstacles, shatters them apart,
brings about the destruction of all enemies, and annihilates even great death.
[He is] the destroyer of wrinkles, graying hair, misfortune, old age, and disease;
the god Bhairava, who bestows all accomplishments and protects his devotees.
Hara, the teacher of all the worlds, whose three eyes are adorned and filled with the essence of honey, and whose mind is characterized by supreme bliss.
For the pacification of all obstacles, one should meditate with one-pointed intellect upon that goddess Caṇḍikā,
the destroyer of suffering, who resides upon the ground during that hour.
She resembles a dark cloud or collyrium; her hair is curly and stands upright;
she is adorned with a garland of skulls and decorated with earrings of serpents.
Adorned with red perfumes, flowers, and other ornaments,
she has six faces and twelve arms, with a tooth-mark upon each lip.
She holds a vajra, a goad, an excellent discus, a wheel, a sword, a shield, and a trident; she bears a battle-axe, a staff, a mace, and displays the gestures of granting boons and fearlessness.
I bow to the auspicious one, the three-eyed, the destroyer of the afflictions of her devotees, whose crest is the moon;
she who removes the threefold suffering of her devotees and whose form is the devourer of Time.
[I praise] Bhairavī, who removes all fear, who is rich with skull-bowls full of honey-wine, who dwells in fresh youth, and who is attended by hosts of Yoginīs.
A yogi, for the sake of attaining the fruits of yoga, should thus meditate for a long time upon the Goddess, the triad of causes that brings about the attainment of all desired results.
For the sake of pacifying all calamities and for the attainment of all desired fruits,
by means of this yoga of meditation, [one is protected] even from the fear of timely death.
O Supreme Goddess, one is liberated; what I have spoken cannot be false.
This "Asi" is the great meditation, from which all afflictions and doubts have been abandoned.
Furthermore, for the pacification of all calamities, one should meditate upon Mahādeva within the lotus of the heart— Mahādeva, whose radiance is equal to the rising sun.
The God, whose body was embraced by the Goddess who was of an identical golden complexion,
bore ashes smeared over all his limbs and wore a tiger skin.
Seated in the lotus posture, peaceful, three-eyed, and moon-crested;
his divine forehead marked by the young moon and drenched in flowing nectar.
I bow to the auspicious Supreme Lord, who holds the boon-granting gesture, the gesture of fearlessness, the great mace, and the deer-mark; who bears a rosary and a book, and is serene.
Possessing a mass of matted locks adorned with a great jewel,
endowed with fresh youth, and having swallowed fear and other afflictions of the world.
With a beautiful face and lovely limbs in every part, his sphere of activity is hidden wisdom;
he is the shatterer of the bonds that bind living beings and the savior from the ocean of worldly existence.
One should meditate thus upon Mahādeva, the bestower of the power of the qualities of omniscience and the giver of all accomplishments, for the pacification of all obstacles.
For the attainment of omniscience and as the sole cause for all success,
or else in another manner, one should meditate for the sake of the pacification of suffering.
Resembling pure crystal, with the radiance of ten thousand autumn moons,
holding a rosary, peaceful, with a serene countenance, and auspicious.
Combined with the three-pronged [vajra] and the gesture of fearlessness, it possesses a radiance like silver and other such metals;
it pacifies all death and destroys wrinkles and graying hair.
He was showering divine nectar from all sides with great rains;
by the sudden falling of that shower of ambrosia, which was cooling to the soul, [the world was refreshed].
One should meditate upon one's own body as being entirely free from the nature of suffering;
by means of this yoga of meditation, one is liberated from the bondage of suffering.
O Pārvatī, when a yogi perceives an obstacle that has arisen from diseases, calamities, or likewise from the lord of the Guhyakas;
Then the wise one should offer the bali-oblation according to the previously mentioned procedure,
by means of the previously mentioned recitations and fire-offerings, as well as the medicinal herbs to be described hereafter.
One should pacify any obstacle that has arisen through gifts, fire-offerings, and likewise through meditations.
Thus ends the twelfth chapter, titled "The Pacification of Obstacles," in the Yogasārasaṃgraha.
The bases are said by yogis to be ninety-six in all bodies;
having summarized them, I shall describe the six bases in their proper order.
The Ādhāra, Maṇipūra, Svādhiṣṭhāna, Anāvṛta, Viśuddhi, and Ājñā— these six cakras are proclaimed as the Mādhāraṇī.
In the *Rudrarahasya*:
"Since the earth is the support of all, it exists as the *mūlādhāra*;
by its absence, there would be the fall of the body from its state of upward emergence."
In the *Yājñavalkya*: "Two finger-breadths above the anus and two finger-breadths below the penis—
the space between these two is declared to be the *mūlādhāra* for human beings."
p.
71) For quadrupeds, however, it is the center of the heart; for animals that crawl, it is the center of the belly.
—From the *Yogasāramañjarī*:
That which is situated in the center of the support of the liṅga, in the middle of the śakti and accompanied by the kuṇḍalinī,
measuring one barley-corn in size and of excellent triangular form.
That state is partless, radiant energy, and is designated as "higher than the high."
In the *Praṇavacintāmaṇi*:
"In the center of the body, at the place of fire, [is the seat] with the radiance of molten gold;
it is triangular for bipeds and quadrangular for quadrupeds."
For birds it is circular; for those born from eggs, hexagonal;
for those born from sweat, octagonal; and within that, [for those born from moisture], it is as radiant as a lamp.
In the *Jñānavidyā*:
"Śakti is known to have the form of a triangle, and Śiva has the form of a bindu;
therefore, there is a relationship of inseparable concomitance (*avinābhāva*) between the bindu and the triangle."
And from the Yogārṇava:
"In the center of the earth-lotus, one should visualize the circle of fire, conjoined with the quality of rajas; in its center is Parameṣṭhin."
Thus, the great liṅga Bimba is the abode of Śiva and Śakti;
it is the station of Śiva in the form of the individual soul (jīva), which illuminates that very state.
Wherein the supreme power named Kuṇḍalinī is established,
from that wind arises, and from that fire is born.
From that the *bindu* arises, from which the *nāda* proceeds;
from that the *sūrya* arises, and from that the mind (*manas*) arises.
"This very seat, known as Kāmarūpa, bestows the fruit of desire. Thus [it is said].
The Mūlādhāra is a threefold circle, the Brahma-cakra, which is like a tree;
the Śakti situated below the *kanda* has a radiance equal to the rising sun.
It has four petals and four colors, with the luster of molten gold.
It consists of four quarters, is supreme bliss, adorned with the four traditions (āmnāyas),
filled with fifty-six kalās, and enveloped by the measures of fragrance (gandhamātrā).
The extent of the terrestrial circle has been thus described by the ancients;
because it is filled with jewels (*maṇi*), it is remembered as Maṇipūraka.
The ocean is filled with jewels; therefore, it is called Maṇipūraka. It is the sphere of Varuṇa, whose presiding deity is Viṣṇu, the essence of sattva.
"Joined with a white banner and saturated with the nectar of the citron"—
thus it is stated in the scriptures within the sections concerning the purification of the marvelous (*adbhutaśuddhi*).
Thus [it was] given by Datta.

The state of authoritativeness is the illusion of Viṣṇu, consisting of pure qualities; it is a six-spoked [wheel], a six-petalled lotus, possessing a clear luster, having six syllables, accompanied by the wealth of Śiva, and served by powers.
It is situated within the seed-syllable, is a citron, the abode of the Lord of Rati, and has the nature of a crescent moon—this is the sacred place.
This wheel is filled with jewels that are suns for the arrival of living beings.
(As stated) in the *Laharī*:

"It is filled with five hundred and two *kalās*. In the *Yogadīpikā*, it is called *svādhiṣṭhāna* because, having formed a knot of the *kuṇḍalinī*, it remains presiding over itself (*sva-adhiṣṭhāya sthitatvāt*).
As it has been stated in the *Yogayātrākalkya*:
"The location of the *kanda* for human beings is nine finger-breadths within the center of the body;
its height is four finger-breadths, and its length is likewise the same."
Adorned with a circle of fire having the shape of an egg, the wheel is endowed with twelve spokes; by that, it is established within the body.
Driven by merit and demerit, the living being revolves in this wheel,
just as a spider moves within the midst of its web of threads.
"In this mūlādhāra-cakra of the living being (jīva), these vital breaths (prāṇas) move below;
the jīva is always mounted upon the prāṇa within all beings. Thus says Gorakṣa. And in the Mahābhārata:
Between the samāna and vyāna breaths, the prāṇa and apāna move about;
when one is asleep, both the samāna and the vyāna dissolve into that [prāṇa].
"Udāna stands pervading the space between the apāna and the prāṇa;
therefore, it does not leave the sleeping person. Thus, according to the Śruti, the vital breaths (prāṇas) do not abandon the sleeping person."
In the *Saundaryalaharī*:
"The earth is at the *mūlādhāra*, fire resides somewhere in the *maṇipūra*,
the vital air is situated in the *svādhiṣṭhāna*, and space is above in the heart."
The sequence of the Mūlādhāra and Svādhiṣṭhāna [cakras], concerning the knots of the heart and other objects.
In the section on the zodiacal wheel (*rāśicakra*), Yājñavalkya states that the navel-wheel (*nābhicakra*) has twelve spokes.
Within the center of the pair of wheels through the division of the wheel of withdrawal (*saṃhāracakra*),
the form of Rudra himself resides within the bodies of all living beings.
As it is stated in the Yogaśāṅkara:
"Placing the earth, which pervades the cosmic egg, into the midst of water;
having placed the essence (rasa) in fire, one should place the water into the midst of air."
"O Śiva, having drawn in the wind from space, it is released again. Thus it is said.
The Mūlādhāra and Svādhiṣṭhāna are declared to be the Rudra-knot;
the Maṇipūra and Anāhata are clearly known as the Viṣṇu-knot.
"The three knots are declared to be named Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Śiva through their purity.
Thus [it is said]. Svādhiṣṭhāna has ten spokes and is endowed with ten powers;
it is a reddish circle of fire, with Rudra as its presiding deity.
The mandala of the Svādhiṣṭhāna consists of the seed-syllable RAṂ, endowed with three qualities, joined with triangles and svastikas,
and possessed of sixty-two karaṇas.
The yogi who performs this in reverse does not perish;
he becomes the agent of creation, maintenance, and dissolution—of this there is no doubt.
It is called *anāhata* because it is not struck (*na āhata*).
For what reason? Because that which is struck is gross and manifold, whereas this is not struck.
Therefore, it was declared by the sages of old that this is the unstruck (nāhata) heart.
Śiva said: One should know that the stalk of knowledge (vidyā-nāla), which extends from the root-kanda to the tip of the experience, exists within the center of the bodies of all beings,
having itself become established as the heart-lotus.
This has been stated by Yogayājñavalkya: "The location of Kuṇḍalī is above the *kanda*, situated transversely and extending downward from the navel.
She is radiant like a streak of lightning situated in the midst of dark blue clouds.
Thin like the awn of wild rice, yellow, radiant, and peerless.
Within the fire of that crest-lock, the Supreme Self is established.
In the *Yogasāramañjarī*:
"The root of the star [the *tāraka*] is situated at the heart-lotus, with the *śakti* as its stalk;
it is enriched with petals from the circle of fire and has the solar orb as its filaments."
The filaments of the lunar mandala are the pericarp of the supreme temple.
Ādinātha:
Born from the bulbous root of Brahmā, it has the stalk of knowledge, is beautiful to the wise,
is endowed with the eight petals of sovereignty, and has supreme detachment as its pericarp.
"Having fashioned the pedestal of the lotus-foot, which has the form of the eight Bhūtikās, is joined with the moon and fire of compassion, and is well-served by the three forms;
[the lotus] has four petals in its lower part and likewise eight petals above."
The eight-spoked wheel of the yoga of meditation is like the sun within the *mātṛkā*.
The six-cornered wind is smoke-colored and endowed with the quality of touch alone.
The abode of the Lord is adorned with fifty-four rays,
being especially pure at all times among all beings.
Therefore, it is renowned as pure, the domain of pure consciousness;
it is a pure sixteen-petaled lotus adorned with the sixteen vowels,
situated at the uvula (ghaṇṭikā) based upon the root of the uvula.
Therein is the mandala of Ākāra, the abode of Sadāśiva,
complete with sixteen digits (kalās) and likewise with sixteen powers (śaktis).
Resembling a dark blue cloud and attended by the vital breath udāna,
the goddess of speech named Vaikharī was born from that and became widespread.
This wheel of grace is always served by the deities of the directions;
its luminous nature, as it exists in dreams, is proclaimed in the Brahmopaniṣad.
That from the knowledge of which everything arises, by virtue of being the locus and cause of that knowledge,
is called the *ājñācakra*, situated between the eyebrows of all embodied beings.
They perceive something in the throat, but nothing at all in the heart;
from the middle of the eyebrows, however, everything is known— therefore it is called the "Command" (ājñā).
As it is said in the Āśvalāyanopaniṣad:
"One should know the waking state to be in the eyes, and one should designate the dreaming state as being in the throat.
The Ājñā-cakra is located between the eyebrows; it has two petals and is endowed with two syllables.
Endowed with two powers and possessed of the Brahma-knot,
the Kolāṭa-maṇḍala is situated there, possessing a radiance equal to ten million moons.
Pervaded by qualities such as rajas and manifesting in various colors,
that Lord of the Universe dwells there within embodied beings under the name Viśva.
This is stated in the Jābāla Upaniṣad:
"The junction between the eyebrows and the nose is indeed the junction of the heavenly world;
the knowers of Brahman worship this junction as the twilight (saṃdhyā)."
"He is established in Avimukta. In the *Yogasāramañjarī*:

"O Supreme Goddess, the divine city of Vārāṇasī is on the forehead," [and] according to the Teachers: "[The deity] residing in your command-wheel (ājñācakra), possessing the brilliance of ten million moons and suns."

The elements, beginning with space, underwent transformation through the distinctions of their functions such as supporting and so forth, as well as through the distinctions of their qualities such as sound and the rest.
As it is said in the Vāsiṣṭha:
"The five elements are present everywhere; there is nothing whatsoever as a sixth.
Having understood this, one should then open the doors of the six supports (ādhāras).
The thousand-spoked wheel is said to be her own nature in the section concerning Kuṇḍalinī.
Thus ends the thirteenth chapter, titled "The Description of the Six Supports," in the *Yogasārasaṃgraha*.

He describes the nature of Kuṇḍalinī: "Within the body-egg, in the center of the wheel, she who occupies the hollow of the lotus-fiber shines like a flash of lightning or a manifest creeper, always within the interior of the womb of embodied beings."

Residing in the *mūlādhāra*, she is the triple-formed Mother, the power (*śakti*) of the Supreme Brahman, the coiled one (*kuṇḍalinī*), the progenitor of the three worlds, and the savorer of the nectar of the void.
Kuṇḍalī, Suphaṇī, Nāgī, Cakreśvarī, Sarasvatī, Lalanā, Rasanā, Kṣetrā, Lalāṭā, and Śakticālinī.
Rājī, Bhujaṅgī, Śeṣā, Kujāhvā,
Sarpiṇī, Phaṇī, Ādhāraśakti, Kuṭilā, Karalā, and Prāṇavāhinī.
She has eight faces, six supports, is all-pervading, and is the bearer of creative ideation.
The young maiden, whose nature is consciousness, is a key difficult to be understood even by gods and asuras;
she is auspicious, unconditioned by space, time, and the like, and she pervades the meaning of all the Vedas.
This supreme power is remembered as being divided into the higher and the lower;
she dances within the hearts of yogis, eager for the dance.
O Goddess, the auspicious one who consists of all mantras, throbbing with the form of lightning, is the support of all beings and proceeds by way of the spiral of a conch shell.

The Goddess, the Mother, who consists of all reality, is directly manifest; she is the all-pervasive one, composed of the subtlest of the subtle, the three-nights (Triyāmā), whose very nature is the Word-Brahman (Śabdabrahman).
The Supreme Deity Kuṇḍalinī consists of twenty-four syllables and takes the form of fifty letters;
multiplied throughout all her limbs, she pervades everything.
The one whose self is awakened, with a face toward all things, views this moving world as a single string of jewels;
she is the power multiplied into oneness, the impeller of the entire universe.
She is the source of all mantras, the glory of them all, and the very nature of all tantras;
she consists of will, knowledge, and action, and is the embodiment of splendor and the essence of the qualities.
The garland of fifty letters, multiplied by fifty gates, is pure,
consisting of the nature of fire and moon, and having the form of the moon, sun, and fire.
Thus [ends the section on] the names of Kuṇḍalinī.
Now, I shall fully explain the sequence for the arousal of Kuṇḍalinī,
which is difficult for all the wicked to attain, along with the method of recitation for those seeking accomplishment.
In the Vāmakeśvara Mahātantra:
"The Power called Kuṇḍalinī, beautiful like a lotus fiber, is said to reside at the Mūlādhāra in the form of a coiled serpent."
Having bitten the root-tuber with the tip of its hood like a lotus-stalk,
and grasping the tail with its mouth, it is joined to the aperture of Brahma (brahmarandhra).
In the *Yogayājñavalkya*: "A wheel endowed with twelve spokes is established in the region of the navel;
above it is the location of Kuṇḍalinī, which extends obliquely, downward, and upward from the navel."
Consisting of the nature of the eightfold prakṛti, that Kuṇḍalinī is coiled eightfold;
she eternally causes the movement of the vital winds and the [internal] fires according to their proper course.
Constantly remaining, she blocks him from all sides at the flanks of the *kanda*,
likewise completely enveloping the opening of the *brahmarandhra* with her very mouth.
At the time of yoga, she who is awakened by the downward breath (apāna) through water and fire,
resounding in the space of the heart, is of the form of a serpent and intensely radiant.
O friend of the wind, the vital breath does not go through the suṣumnā at all from there.
In the *Praṇavacintāmaṇi*:
"There, having mentally superimposed the fire together with the friend of the wind (the air), one should restrain it;
then, one should always meditate upon the unawakened Kuṇḍalinī situated at the navel within the wheel."
One should not encircle the middle and other parts with the mouth or the body, nor likewise the veins;
rather, having properly seized one's own tail with the mouth and restrained the steps, one should control the hosts of Maruts.

Breathing like a lordly serpent that has awakened, ever-unawakened yet blazing with splendor, that Kuṇḍalī always resides in the navel; she is likewise found horizontally in humans as well as in others.

Know that Kuṇḍalinī, seated upon the lotus-throne which is the support and the cause of arising, destruction, and persistence, filling the apertures; she is the primordial root who bestows the desired perfections of yoga and is firmly established therein.

When the flame of the fire, fanned by the vital wind, abides within the channels situated in the center of the *kanda*, it burns the *Kuṇḍalinī* in its own form; at that time, one indeed does not remember any other object.
There, scorched by the wind and heated by fire,
the serpent with its hood spreads wide and quickly awakens.
When the Wheel-Turner (the soul) has awakened in the center of the navel, all the vital breaths (prāṇas), having fully gathered together in this body,
move along with the fire, just as threads follow the movement of a shuttle.
Having thus conquered the station of Cakriṇī,
one who is devoted to meditation should then lead [the breath] upward from the navel, while recollecting Apāna.
In the *Yogasāramañjarī*:
When the breath, together with its friend the wind, has passed beyond the navel into the body,
diseases perish, strength increases, and at that time, radiant luster awakens.

The mantra-winds, gathered together, proceed with the fire toward the opening of the *brahmarandhra*. I shall tell you this by some means here, as it has been seen in my heart like a lamp in the presence of Śiva.
O best of the twice-born, that [wind] should then be restrained within the heart by means of that wind which is its companion;
having entered the mouth of the thousand-petaled lotus, it should again be made to face upward.
When the lotus of the heart had awakened within that city of Brahmā,
the wind shone like a row of birds in the sky.
They say that the Fire-eater (Agni) is situated within the Suṣumṇā;
he shines like a streak of lightning amidst garlands of water-bearing clouds.

O Dear One, having attained the state of *kumbhaka* (retention) after the two channels consisting of the moon and the sun have been ceased, one whose mind is steady and whose posture is firm [should proceed].
And having restrained the mind within one's own heart, at the base of the earth in the *mūlādhāra*,
situated in the midst of the city of the heart’s corner, within the solar and lunar orbs that flow [there].
Having the form of a serpent in deep sleep, she is the supreme one consisting of all mantras;
she pierces the three knots at the junctions of the *ilā* and *piṅgalā* channels.
Capable of opening the door-panel of the cave-passage of the six lotuses,
let it be gradually raised from its root and established in the *ājñā* [cakra];
then, having pierced the great bolt of Śiva’s door with the tongue [of the vital breath].
Fixing one's gaze upon the aperture of Brahma (brahmarandhra) and making the mind steady within the heart,
there too, O Goddess, is the triangle (śṛṅgāṭa), a mandala exceedingly brilliant.
One should know the triangle to contain within it fire, sun, and moon;
therein, within the lunar orb, resides the Goddess, the Supreme Self, Sadāśiva.
As long as the Supreme Lord does not attain union with His own power (Śakti),
so long He causes the universe to revolve, mounted upon a machine by means of Māyā.
Śiva:
O Lord, the supreme Śakti Kuṇḍalinī, rising from the Mūlādhāra,
then becomes perfectly upward-facing through the utterance of her own mantra.
Emerging from the sound of six *huṃ* syllables, she shattered the divine bolt of Brahmā with her six-armed door-bolt and, having broken through it, returned to her own abode.
Having pierced through the circles of fire and sun, they flow toward the lunar orb.
The nectar arising from that has a delicious taste and delights in supreme bliss.
A woman of noble family, having abandoned her own family,
went to another man who was without distinguishing marks, devoid of virtues, and bereft of noble birth and beauty.
There, assuming a form at her own will, she embraces her own husband and,
delighted by the joy of his enjoyment, rests for a long time.
Constantly sprinkling the body of the yogin with supreme showers of rain,
she returns to her own husband by the very path through which he has gone.
By this yoga, O Goddess, one becomes a lord of yogins within a month;
after six months, one becomes the master of the supernatural powers, beginning with *aṇimā*.
One who drinks even the ocean playfully every day for a year [attains] the gradual power to arrest the waters of the sun, wind, fire, and so forth.
By the power of Rudra’s energy, the yogi performs [these feats] with ease;
having become omniscient within three years, he is freed from wrinkles and grey hair.
Possessing great strength and a vajra-body, he shall live as long as the moon and stars;
this great yoga of the Śakti-mantra has been taught to you, O lady of excellent vows.

The Knower of the Field (kṣetrajña), who is the vehicle of the vital breath (prāṇavāhana), [perceives] his own self as the individual soul (jīvātman) within all these— the vowels, mantras, Purāṇas, and qualities— in every respect.
"The universe is within the Suṣumnā; everything is established in it. Thus [it is said]. In the *Cintātimirabhāskara*:
"Resorting to Meru within the body like a jeweled staff..."
The auspicious Suṣumnā exists within the body, resembling a lotus fiber.
From Brahma down to a blade of grass, consciousness exists within them all; that which shines forth as their beginning, middle, and end is designated as "citta."
"You shine like the flame of a lamp situated within a jar that has a hole;
thus, O dear son, it is said that the interior of the nature of the individual soul (jīva) is pervaded.
Thus [it is stated] in the Yājñavalkya.

Extending from the tip of the corner of the *mūlādhāra* to the end of the twelve [finger-breadths] at the top of the *suṣumnā*, resembling a bamboo stalk cut off at its base, it is called the *brahmanāḍī*. Its cavity is subtle; in it, everything is established.
Beyond the four locations at the end of the head, further upward,
is the place known as the "twelve-finger limit" (dvādaśānta), where the Supreme Self is established.
Below that, the power Unmanī resides at a distance of four finger-breadths;
the power named Samanā is well-established there as that very power.
"Three finger-breadths below [the navel], it shines with the splendor of a hundred thousand suns;
from the head down to the position of the fingers, that very power is the radiant *suprabhā*.
Thus it is said in the *Tantrasāra*.
From that Śiva, the supreme Śakti is born with a thousandth part [of his essence];
she is designated as Śakti by various names such as Śānti and others, though much could be said.
As it is stated in the Mṛgendra-tantra: "And that Kuṇḍalinī is the pure power (śakti) of Śambhu, whose nature is Iḍā."
That very [consciousness], while existing as the present state of appropriation, does not abide as the self of that [body],
because it is the material cause of the body, just as clay is the material cause of a potter's vessel.
In the thousand-spoked [cakra], at the tip of two finger-breadths, the Śakti always resides like a jewel-staff, joined with two dots on both sides.
"Three finger-breadths below the *daṇḍa*, at the tip of the *bindu* and the middle of the *ardhacandra*,
the power known as *nirodhinī* always resides. Thus it is said in the *Antasāra*.
Three finger-breadths in width at the forehead and one foot in height,
the divine liṅga is perfectly formed and possesses a radiance like that of the half-moon.
Thus it is said in the *Yogasāramañjarī*:
"O Supreme Goddess, on the forehead is the divine city of Avārāṇasī;
there reside the mantras Avarṇa, Ananta, Viraja, and Sarasvatī."
Within a two-finger circle between the eyebrows, she possesses a radiance equal to that of a lamp.
Śiva, as Someśvara, is situated at the confluence of the white and black rivers;
and thus says the Śruti:
"Where the Gaṅgā and Yamunā meet, where the Prācī Sarasvatī flows..."
Where the god Someśvara is, there indeed the Self is of the nature of nectar.
Then, in the sheath of the fingers, there is the one with the luster of the sun and moon, measuring two finger-breadths;
Māyā, the principle of poison, and Rudra are situated in the region of the throat.
In the Dakṣiṇāmūrtikalpa:
"Above the navel, at a distance of one span, is the heart, four finger-breadths in size;
situated at its end is Medhā, whose form is like fire and whose radiance is equal to it."
"In the center of the navel-circle, however, Icchā and Vidyā are established.
Below that, at the tip of Maṇipūra, resides the Lord of Pleasure and Displeasure.
In the Mūlādhāra resides the power Kuṇḍalinī, the supreme deity.
In the *Yogasāramañjarī*:
Now, O Maheśvarī, the door of the bolt of Brahman (*brahmārgaladvāra*) is difficult to discern;
situated therein is the supreme quartet of *kalās*, which consists of the four aims of human life (*caturvarga*).
In the eastern part is the one named Amṛtā; Guptā resides in the southern region;
Śivā is in the western direction; and Parāparā is in the north, O Śiva.
When the yogi pierces that door with the tip of his tongue and drinks the nectar of the primordial digit (*apūrvakalāmṛta*),
he indeed becomes a lord within half a month.
Just as a skillful yogi might lick hidden nectar with his tongue,
O God, in one month— without a doubt— he shall become a manifest Lord of Half [the Universe].

By withdrawing [the breath] into the western *kalā*, one becomes Kāmeśvara; by withdrawing it into the northern *kalā*, one attains the state of Parameṣṭhin. Above that, in the mandala, the supreme nectar is dissolved within the *brahmaraṃdhra*.
Merely by drinking that nectar, a living being becomes liberated and attains the state of Śiva.
Therein, O Īśvarī, they call the summit Cūlitala and say it is Kedāra.
In that regard, O Goddess worshipped by heroes, the eight digits of the Moon are renowned as Amṛtā, Ānadā, Pūṣā, Tuṣṭi, Puṣṭi, Rati, and Dhṛti.

From the drawing in of the digits beginning with Śaśinī, the state of moving through the sky (khecaratva) arises. It is taught that one should bend [the gaze] toward the space between the eyebrows; that is declared to be the lunar orb (somamaṇḍala).
The digits beginning with Candrikā are said to be the abode of supreme nectar (parāmṛta).
He who drinks that with his tongue possesses a body as firm as a thunderbolt.
Above that, situated between the *śilā* and the *khecarī*, is that which is called the *vajrakanda*;
one should know that to be the forehead (*lalāṭa*), the locus of the divine powers (*devikalā*). Because it has drawn forth those initial powers, it cannot be pierced by missiles or weapons.
It is inconceivable by all forms of consciousness associated with their respective objects.
If there is enjoyment of Bhairava, it is true by the power of the Vajra-root,
on the great path of the royal tooth, below the nose and above the lower lip.
There, having attained the state of *kumbhaka*, one should touch with the tip of the tongue that pair of digits which bestow the full nectar of desire.
By drinking that nectar for two months, all disease is destroyed;
it is situated between the anus and the genitals, conceived as the *ādhāra*.
Therein, the five *kalās* are proclaimed as previously [described]: Prāgutpattā, Paramāmṛtā, Sudhā, Sudhāmayī, and Prājñā; [they are] Kālaghnī and Jñānadāyinī.
These five *kalās*, which are streams of nectar, are celebrated as bestowing all spiritual accomplishments (*siddhis*).
O Goddess worshipped by the gods, the supreme power Māyā-kuṇḍalinī resides there within Śiva; [she is awakened] there through the yoga of contraction and by means of breath-retention (kumbhaka).
Having tasted the cool nectar located there with the Root Power (mūla-śakti),
one should draw it upward through the Suṣumṇā from the lotuses of the Svādhiṣṭhāna and other centers,
and contemplate it as sprinkling a rain of that nectar as far as the limits of the Brahmāṇḍa.
There, the supreme Śakti, the venerable Kuṇḍalinī, having taken up the nectar situated therein,
reaches the end of the abode of Brahman by following the path of the Suṣumṇā.
Through practice for five months, mastery over the five elements will occur;
one will truly become equal to Śiva through the yoga of practice throughout the three periods of time.
p. 89) For the place of the navel, O Goddess, is called by me Svādhiṣṭhāna;
there, the three digits consisting of divine nectar are proclaimed.
Suṣumnā is proclaimed as the supreme bliss and as Vidyā;
having attained the state of kumbhaka as before, one awakens the Śakti.
By merely drinking that nectar, one attains the fruit previously described.
That which is between the anus and the genitals is indeed called the bamboo-staff (veṇudaṇḍa).
Therein, the fourfold *kalā* is said to be the elixir (*rasāyana*) of supreme nectar;
it is intensely cooling, brings great rain, destroys graying hair, and removes wrinkles.
"Having awakened the power (*śakti*) therein, one should flood the body as before;
by practicing this for four months, one attains the fruit previously described. Thus it is said in the *Yogaśāṅkara*.
Hereafter, I shall describe the great path of supreme nectar,
which, within the *vajra-kanda* at the forehead, resembles a blazing moon.
In that square inner sanctum (garbha) resides the supreme deity, Paraśiva;
the Yoginīs worship him there, united with Śakti.
O Great Goddess, upon the surface of the crest, within a triangular maṇḍala possessing a radiance equal to a hundred thousand suns, is the central deity Śiva in the form of the Liṅga;
O Goddess, he is the supreme one, containing the syllable *raṃ* in his center, embraced by his own Śakti.
I meditate upon the Supreme Goddess, who is attended by hosts of deities;
on her auspicious right shank is a six-pointed mark adorned with a circle.
O Goddess, one should meditate upon that smoke-colored embryo as the god Maheśvara there, in the form of a *liṅga*, joined with Śakti and surrounded by his attendants.

O Śivā, in the circle on the left conch, which has the luster of the moon and a lotus, there is the syllable *yaṃ* as the womb and *ṭhaṃ* as the foot in the center; therein is the liṅga consisting of nectar.
Having the appearance of cow’s milk and the brilliance of ten thousand autumn moons,
he is embraced by his own Śakti and served by all the hosts of deities.
Thus, O Goddess, the locations in the four directions have indeed been described by me;
in their midst, O Pārvatī, is the great enclosure, the Haṃsagarbha, where Khageśvara, whose sound is supreme, abides embraced by his own Śakti.
Having the form of a *liṅga* and accompanied by the Gaṇas, with a radiance equal to ten million suns,
he is the youthful Lord of the Earth, the Sun-leader in the west.
In the right conch is Nīlavatī, in the left is Śiva, the Lord of Water;
in the center is Śambhu, the Lord of Space—thus the five locations have been declared.
In the *Yogasāramañjarī*: Four finger-breadths above the head of the Lord, the Sovereign of the Sky,
is [the form] situated in the midst of a circle of light, possessing a radiance equal to ten million moons.
The vessel consists of divine nectar, its base secured by a locking bolt;
it is sealed above by a great mountain, impenetrable, and the abode of immortality.
In the midst of the Śītalā enclosure, the Lord’s Liṅga is dissolved;
it resembles the pollen of three lotuses and possesses a splendor equal to ten million moons.
Free from rejection and acceptance, dispelling the darkness of ignorance,
and transcending the five stages, [this is] for the realization of the supreme reality.
It has a door-panel that serves as a vessel for the supreme nectar and is provided with water-pots.
Together with the mind, one should extend the Mistress of Speech (Vāgīśī) with her face turned upward;
that yogi, by means of the tongue, [should move] the throat according to the flow of the vital breath (prāṇa).
Having suddenly attained the nectar of truth, he would effortlessly reveal it;
for there, my nectar is indeed like milk, as sweet as the taste of cool sugarcane juice.
One should drink the midday yogic draught, which is difficult to obtain even for the gods;
and being satiated by that rain of nectar, one attains the supreme state.
Having attained union there with the *unmanī* state within the interior of the cosmic egg (*brahmāṇḍa*),
the yogi should, through yoga, cause the flesh consisting of *nāda* and *bindu* to expand.
This secret, O Queen of Gods, is difficult to obtain, O Supreme Goddess;
one should meditate upon Vāgīśī, who possesses the luster of ten million moons, upon the tip of the tongue.
Satiated by the digit of supreme nectar, one attains poetic power in an instant;
Fortune, gladdened by the supreme nectar, remains stationed upon the tip of the tongue.
Meditating thus, O Maheśānī, the yogi shall attain the sovereignty of yoga.
Within this supreme self, the body, there are five renowned innate [powers].
When that body was born from the mother’s womb and the father’s seed,
she came to exist together with it as it attained growth.
The primordial Kuṇḍalinī energy is the first, existing as the innate;
the second is named Suṣumnā, and the third is indeed the tongue.
The fourth is the palate as its locus, and the fifth is the locus of Brahmā;
together with Unmanā, one should enter the second Sahajā, which is Māyā.
One should enter the third *sahajā* above;
having pierced the fourth *sahajā*, one should enter the fifth *sahajā*.
Thus has the division been proclaimed by me, O Mistress of the Kula, which is difficult to discern.
From the root, the Kuṇḍalinī energy has entered the path of the Suṣumṇā.
The single thread of the lineage, an image possessing a radiance equal to ten million suns,
shall enter the path of the uvula and pass through the bolt of the door of Śiva.
Thus has this division been proclaimed by me, which is difficult to comprehend, O Maheśvarī;
one should enter the self-existent abode, O beloved, which possesses the splendor of ten million suns.
There, in that great ocean of nectar, garlanded with cool waves,
one should drink the ambrosia and rest; then, with an intellect filled with supreme bliss, one should permeate the body of the self with that nectar until it is satiated.
O Goddess, by means of this yoga, divine vision arises;
the state of being a sky-walker (khecarī) occurs instantly, and there shall be the destruction of all suffering.
He becomes a perfected one (siddha) who certainly deceives death and time, who is the unique jewel of the three worlds, and who is endowed with the qualities such as atomization (aṇimā).
One attains the state of a lord of yogins, and the infamy of one's intellect is destroyed;
nor is one [overpowered] even by oneself, though accompanied by the strength of thousands of nāgas.
The yogi is born like Śiva; this is the truth, the truth that I have declared.
Śiva:
Having arisen from the *mūlādhāra*, piercing the six door-panels and breaking through the divine bolt of Brahmā, she has ascended to the station of the sleeping Lord.
Having pierced the orbs of fire and sun, she flows toward the orb of the moon;
tasting the nectar arising therefrom, she is gladdened by supreme bliss.
The woman of the Kula, having abandoned the Kula, has reached the Supreme Puruṣa.
There, devoid of marks, devoid of qualities, and free from family and form, she—
possessing a form of her own free will— embraced her husband.
Having rested for a long time, she, delighted by the bliss of those enjoyments,
constantly sprinkles the body of the yogi with supreme showers.
Just as one returns to one's own place by the same path by which one went.
Thus ends the fifteenth chapter, titled "The Description of the Nature of the Kalās of Suṣumnā," in the Yogasārasaṃgraha.
Now, the locations of the living soul within the body and the nature of the individual self (jīvātman) are described— in the Śivayoga:
"He is established in the foundation (ādhāra), in the heart, and in the place of the head."
Thus was he addressed by Śiva, the Supreme Self, regarding attachment to the body.
In the Brahmopaniṣad it is said:
"One should know that the waking state resides in the eyes; one should designate the dreaming state as being in the throat;
the deep sleep state resides in the heart; and the fourth state (turya) is situated in the head."
Datta says: "Wind, fire, and likewise space—this triad is designated as the *jīva*.
That *jīva* is called *prāṇa*, and it is conceived as being [subtler] than a hundredth part of the tip of a hair."
In the Yājñavalkya-smṛti:
having divided a banyan seed into a hundred parts, [the measure] is equal to one-hundredth part of a single such portion.
The sages declare that a portion of that very [Self] is likewise well-known as the one called the individual soul (jīva).
In the Muṇḍaka Upaniṣad:
"This subtle Self is to be known by the mind,
into which the vital breath has entered fivefold."
The mind of all these living beings is supported by the vital breaths;
within that [breath], this Self becomes purified.
The mind is of the nature of light; through its cessation, one attains one's true nature. Having restrained the vital breaths in the aforementioned locations, one should concentrate the mind there.
One should constantly practice for even a moment as a lion against the elephant of death;
through the complete restraint of the vital breaths, the knowledge of one's true nature is accomplished.
In the Brahmopaniṣad:
"Therefore, liberation is desired for this mind when it is devoid of objects."

In the *Uttaragītā*: "Just as water poured into water, milk into milk, or ghee into ghee becomes indistinguishable, so it is with the individual self (*jīvātman*) and the supreme self (*paramātman*). (p. 92)
And so says the Śruti: "Just as when a pot containing space is being carried away, the pot is carried away but not the space; even so, O Bhīṣma, the individual soul [is not carried away].
In the Kaṭhavallī: "This Self is not to be attained by instruction, nor by intellect, nor by much hearing."
Only he whom this Self chooses can obtain it; likewise, the Self chooses him as its own body.
In the *Tāpanīya*: "Om—this single syllable is all this; its further explanation is:
the past, the present, and the future—all this is indeed the syllable Om, as well as whatever else is beyond time."
That too is indeed the syllable *Oṃ*. For all this is Brahman. Now, this Self is Brahman.

This Self is fourfold: the waking-state abode, outwardly conscious, having seven limbs and nineteen mouths, the enjoyer of the gross, Vaiśvānara—this is the first quarter; the dream-state abode, inwardly conscious, having seven limbs...
The third quarter consists of nineteen gates, fourfold in nature, the wise Lord.
He is the ruler of all, he is the all-knowing, he is the inner controller, and he is the source of all; for he is the origin and the dissolution of all beings.
He is not conscious of the external, nor is he unconscious, nor is he devoid of consciousness; he is unseen.

Ineffable, ungraspable, without defining marks, inconceivable, indescribable, having the realization of the one Self as its essence, the cessation of phenomenal expansion, auspicious, and non-dual—this they consider the fourth state; that is the Self, that is to be known. That Self is of the nature of pure consciousness, eternal, all-pervading, changeless, and self-luminous.
The sun of its own nature would illuminate.
Vasiṣṭha says:
That Self which consists of consciousness, is transparent, free from the accumulation of activity, and imperishable—
It is free from that which is to be abandoned and that which is to be grasped, and is unconditioned by place, time, birth, and so forth.
Having attained stability in this fourth state (turya), which is indestructible,
one reaches the station of Great Bliss (mahānanda) by being absorbed into the singular essence of bliss.
Free from beginning and end, truly of the nature of consciousness (cidrūpa), and beyond conceptual construction (nirvikalpaka).
The individual soul (jīva) is the Self that fills space, which is higher than the highest.
He who perceives both himself and the other through the vision of their eternal non-difference,
and sees all as nothing but light— he truly sees.
In the *Avadhūtagītā*:
"Having thus known this path intended for yogins,
this accomplishment, free from conceptual construction, arises of its own accord."
Where there is not even a trace of the various types of channels (nāḍīs), take refuge in the eternal Self, the Lord;
whether one is a practitioner of restraint or not a practitioner of restraint, whether one is free from action or engaged in action.
Through self-awakening, he is certainly liberated; he attains that eternal Lord, the Self.
It is neither mind, nor intellect, nor body, nor sense organ, nor the subtle elements, nor the primordial matter, nor the five gross elements.
Neither "I" nor "the deed" attains that one eternal Self which is their true nature.
Whether at a sacred ford, in his own home, or wherever he may die, the yogi does not enter a womb; he merges into the Supreme Brahman.
Whether at a sacred ford or in the house of an outcaste, abandoning the body while losing consciousness,
one who is liberated at the very moment of realization goes to absolute isolation, with sorrow destroyed.
The mother is purified by noble birth,
and the earth becomes fruitful and prosperous when one’s mind is merged in the Supreme Brahman, this boundless ocean of pure consciousness and bliss.
For all [who listen] to the Yogaśāstra with faith and devotion,
the fruit of a hundred kṛcchra penances is obtained constantly through the mere hearing [of it].
Whoever, endowed with devotion, should read the Yogaśāstra day by day,
for him there is immediate and abundant prosperity therein, and in the end, liberation— of this there is no doubt.
Thus ends the sixteenth chapter, titled "The Determination of the Nature of the Self," in the illustrious *Yogasārasaṃgraha*.
The sequence of the self's abiding state, beginning with Yama and consisting of sixteen further rites,
has been firmly proclaimed across sixteen chapters, supported by many authoritative citations.
Thus ends the *Yogasārasaṃgraha*.
